entries.title: In the beginning
entries.summary: Light breaks into darkness. Genesis opens with a world ordered and called good, and with human beings entrusted with responsibility within it. Jubilees retells creation within a revelation to Moses and gives particular attention to the heavenly world and the Sabbath. Read the accounts alongside one another: the shared story matters, and so do the details each text chooses to tell.
entries.date: Story order · no assigned BCE dates

entries.title: A garden, a choice, an exile
entries.summary: The garden brings the human relationship with God, the earth, and one another into focus. The command, the serpent’s question, and the taking of the fruit lead to shame and expulsion. Jubilees 3 retells the garden story with its own calendar and details. Neither account supplies coordinates that allow us to put a reliable Eden pin on a modern map.
entries.date: Story order · no assigned BCE dates
entries.note: Eden is intentionally unmapped. Proposed modern identifications are not established by the text.

entries.title: A brother’s blood
entries.summary: Cain and Abel bring offerings, but the story turns on anger and the refusal to master it. After Abel’s death, God asks Cain about his brother. The violence of one household becomes a thread running toward the violence of the wider earth before the Flood. Cain’s descendant Enoch is not the Enoch in Seth’s line.
entries.date: Story order · no assigned BCE dates

entries.title: Enoch, who walked with God
entries.summary: Genesis gives Enoch a startlingly brief departure: he walks with God, and God takes him. In 1 Enoch, the same ancestral figure becomes a scribe, intercessor, and witness to heavenly judgment. Jubilees also remembers him as a writer and observer of the heavens. This is Enoch the son of Jared, seventh in the genealogy beginning with Adam—not Cain’s son of the same name.
entries.date: Story order · no assigned BCE dates

entries.title: The Watchers descend
entries.summary: Genesis 6 speaks briefly of the sons of God, human daughters, and the Nephilim. 1 Enoch 6–7 tells a longer account: a group of heavenly beings swears an oath on Mount Hermon, takes wives, and produces destructive giants. The mountain, the oath, and the named leaders come from 1 Enoch; Genesis itself does not supply those details.
entries.date: Story order · no assigned BCE dates
entries.note: This connection compares accounts. It does not treat every interpretation of Genesis’s “sons of God” as identical.

entries.title: Knowledge without wisdom
entries.summary: In 1 Enoch 8, instruction in weapons, adornment, enchantments, and the signs of the heavens becomes part of the world’s corruption. The story asks what happens when knowledge serves violence and domination. These particular teachings and their named teachers belong to the Enochic account; they should not be inserted into Genesis as if Genesis listed them.
entries.date: Story order · no assigned BCE dates

entries.title: The cry of the earth
entries.summary: The suffering earth reaches heaven. 1 Enoch names angelic witnesses who bring the violence before God, then describes judgment on the Watchers and their offspring. Noah is warned of the coming destruction. Enoch later carries a petition from the fallen Watchers, but his answer is not the pardon they seek.
entries.date: Story order · no assigned BCE dates

entries.title: Before the heavenly throne
entries.summary: Enoch’s vision moves through a fearsome heavenly house to the throne of the Great Glory. The scene presents judgment from the viewpoint of heaven rather than from a battlefield or palace. It offers a useful comparison with prophetic throne visions, while its imagery and message remain those of 1 Enoch.
entries.date: Story order · no assigned BCE dates

entries.title: Journeys beyond the familiar world
entries.summary: Enoch is led through places of judgment, mountains, the dwelling places of the dead, and visions of the tree reserved for the righteous. These are visionary journeys, not a travel itinerary we can reliably draw across modern countries. The named guides and landscapes open a window into the book’s moral geography.
entries.date: Story order · no assigned BCE dates
entries.note: Visionary locations are not plotted as surveyed geographic places.

entries.title: The lights and the calendar
entries.summary: The Astronomical Book within 1 Enoch describes heavenly movements under angelic instruction. Jubilees emphasizes a 364-day calendar and the danger of losing the proper order of festivals. Their interest in ordered time connects creation, worship, and faithful living. These ancient accounts are presented as their own textual traditions, not as modern astronomical models.
entries.date: Story order · no assigned BCE dates

entries.title: The astonishing birth of Noah
entries.summary: 1 Enoch 106–107 tells a story absent from Genesis: Lamech is alarmed by his newborn son’s extraordinary appearance and asks Methuselah for help. Methuselah turns to Enoch, who explains the child’s identity and the coming Flood. Keeping the source label visible lets us explore this vivid family story without confusing it with Genesis’s much shorter notice of Noah’s birth.
entries.date: Story order · no assigned BCE dates

entries.title: Noah and a world in crisis
entries.summary: Noah stands at the hinge between the world before the Flood and the families after it. Genesis emphasizes his righteousness, his household, and his obedience in building the ark. The Enochic and Jubilees traditions add further accounts of warning, corruption, and the struggle with evil. His sons Shem, Ham, and Japheth become the starting points of the post-Flood genealogies.
entries.date: Story order · no assigned BCE dates

entries.title: The Flood
entries.summary: Violence has filled the earth. Genesis describes the ark, rising waters, the preservation of living creatures, and the eventual return to dry ground. 1 Enoch and Jubilees connect the catastrophe with the corruption associated with the Watchers. The texts meet around judgment and preservation, though their narrative details are not interchangeable.
entries.date: Story order · no assigned BCE dates

entries.title: A bow in the clouds
entries.summary: After the Flood, the story opens outward to every living creature. Genesis describes a covenant, a prohibition on bloodshed, and the bow in the clouds as its sign. Jubilees 6 connects Noah’s sacrifice and covenant with sacred time and the Feast of Weeks. A new beginning does not erase the need for justice or faithful remembrance.
entries.date: Story order · no assigned BCE dates

entries.title: Noah’s prayer and Mastema
entries.summary: Jubilees 10 returns to the problem of evil after the Flood. Noah prays for his descendants when destructive spirits trouble them. Mastema asks that a portion remain under his authority; the account also describes instruction in healing. This is a distinct Jubilees narrative, useful for seeing how that book carries the consequences of the primeval crisis into later generations.
entries.date: Story order · no assigned BCE dates

entries.title: Families become nations
entries.summary: Genesis 10 arranges the peoples of the world through the descendants of Noah’s sons. Jubilees 8–9 offers its own account of the division of the earth, with boundaries and solemn warnings. These are ancient ways of describing the world and its peoples; they are not modern ethnic classifications or precise national borders.
entries.date: Story order · no assigned BCE dates

entries.title: A city and a scattered people
entries.summary: In the land of Shinar, people build a city and tower to make a name and resist being scattered. The confusion of language turns the project inside out. The next great movement in Genesis is toward one family called to become a blessing for the nations. Jubilees 10 also retells the tower episode.
entries.date: Story order · no assigned BCE dates
entries.note: The map marks Babylon as a regional reference, not the location of an archaeologically identified biblical tower.

entries.title: Leave your country
entries.summary: Abram’s journey begins with a promise that reaches beyond his household: blessing for the families of the earth. Haran, Shechem, Bethel, and Egypt become places where that promise is tested and carried forward. The lines on the atlas connect named destinations; they do not claim to reproduce ancient roads or exact routes.
entries.date: Ancestral narratives · dates debated

entries.title: Abraham and his father’s idols
entries.summary: Jubilees tells more of Abram’s early life than Genesis does. He challenges idol worship and burns the house of idols; his brother Haran dies in the fire. The narrative also describes Abram rejecting dependence on heavenly signs and turning in prayer to the Creator. These episodes belong to Jubilees 12, not to Genesis’s brief genealogy.
entries.date: Ancestral narratives · dates debated

entries.title: A meeting with Melchizedek
entries.summary: After the rescue of Lot, Abram meets Melchizedek, king of Salem and priest of God Most High. Bread, wine, blessing, and a tenth of the spoils mark this short encounter. Psalm 110 and Hebrews later return to this figure; those later readings can be followed without turning the few verses of Genesis into a full biography it does not provide.
entries.date: Ancestral narratives · dates debated
entries.note: Salem is often identified with Jerusalem; the atlas does not require that identification for this encounter.

entries.title: Lot and the cities of the plain
entries.summary: Abraham’s questions about justice lead into the story of Lot, threatened visitors, escape, and the destruction of the cities. Genesis also preserves a difficult account of Lot’s family after the catastrophe. The narrative connects Abraham’s household with the origins of Moab and Ammon, but the cities’ exact locations remain disputed.
entries.date: Ancestral narratives · dates debated

entries.title: Abraham’s test
entries.summary: Genesis presents God testing Abraham in the command concerning Isaac, ending with the provision of a ram. Jubilees 17–18 places the test within a heavenly challenge involving Mastema and adds its own framing. Read them side by side: shared figures and action, but a different account of what precedes the trial.
entries.date: Ancestral narratives · dates debated

entries.title: A stairway at Bethel
entries.summary: On the road away from home, Jacob dreams of a stairway reaching heaven and hears the ancestral promise renewed. He names the place Bethel. Centuries later Bethel becomes a royal sanctuary under Jeroboam. A place of encounter in one generation becomes a place of prophetic dispute in another.
entries.date: Ancestral narratives · dates debated

entries.title: A new name at the river
entries.summary: Before meeting Esau again, Jacob wrestles through the night and receives the name Israel. The reconciliation that follows does not erase the wounds or fears that brought the brothers to this point. The name of one man becomes the name of a people—and later a kingdom—so the atlas keeps those different uses of “Israel” distinct.
entries.date: Ancestral narratives · dates debated

entries.title: The household of Israel
entries.summary: Jacob’s children come through Leah, Rachel, Bilhah, and Zilpah. Their family becomes the basis of the tribal story, but lists of tribes vary with purpose: Levi has a distinct role, and Joseph may be represented by Ephraim and Manasseh. The family tree shows named relationships, not a claim that every biblical tribal list has the same twelve entries.
entries.date: Ancestral narratives · dates debated

entries.title: Joseph is sold
entries.summary: A favored son, dreams, and a bloodied garment tear a household apart. Joseph reaches Egypt through betrayal and sale. Jubilees 34 retells the episode and connects the family’s grief to remembrance. Genesis will later revisit the brothers’ responsibility through Joseph’s own words about preservation and providence.
entries.date: Ancestral narratives · dates debated

entries.title: Tamar interrupts the family story
entries.summary: While Joseph’s story unfolds, Genesis pauses over Judah and Tamar. Denied the future she had been promised, Tamar forces Judah to recognize his own failure. Their son Perez belongs to the genealogy later leading to David. The family line carries difficult stories, not a polished parade of faultless ancestors.
entries.date: Ancestral narratives · dates debated

entries.title: A family preserved in Egypt
entries.summary: Joseph’s rise in Egypt places him in a position to preserve the family during famine. Reconciliation takes time and tests the brothers’ willingness to protect Benjamin. Jacob’s household settles in Egypt, and Genesis ends with Joseph’s death and his request concerning his bones—a promise that reaches into Exodus and Joshua.
entries.date: Ancestral narratives · dates debated

entries.title: A call from the burning bush
entries.summary: Moses encounters a bush burning without being consumed. The call is grounded in God’s attention to the suffering of the enslaved people. Moses objects, asks questions, and is sent back toward Pharaoh with Aaron’s help. Horeb and Sinai are linked in the biblical tradition, but their precise geographical identification remains debated.
entries.date: Exodus chronology and routes debated

entries.title: A night of departure
entries.summary: The confrontation with Pharaoh reaches the night of Passover. A meal, marked doorways, judgment, and hurried departure become a memory to be kept across generations. Jubilees 49 gives its own instruction about observing the festival. The atlas does not identify an unnamed Pharaoh or assign a single settled date to the Exodus.
entries.date: Exodus chronology and routes debated

entries.title: Through the sea
entries.summary: Trapped between the sea and an approaching army, the people pass through on dry ground in Exodus’s account. Moses and Miriam lead songs of deliverance afterward. The Hebrew name Yam Suph is often rendered “Red Sea” or “Sea of Reeds”; the precise crossing site is not established here.
entries.date: Exodus chronology and routes debated
entries.note: No exact crossing point or route is plotted.

entries.title: Covenant at the mountain
entries.summary: Rescue from Egypt leads to a covenant and a way of life. At Sinai the people hear the commandments, and Moses receives instruction for the community. The mountain becomes central to Exodus and to the framing of Jubilees: the latter presents its account of early history as revelation given there.
entries.date: Exodus chronology and routes debated

entries.title: The angel’s account to Moses
entries.summary: Jubilees opens at Sinai, looking backward. God directs Moses to record the divisions of history, and an angel of the presence recounts creation and the generations. That framing explains why Jubilees can sit beside the early Genesis stories in the story view while its scene of revelation belongs here, with Moses.
entries.date: Exodus chronology and routes debated
entries.note: Story setting and the date of a book’s composition are different questions.

entries.title: The calf and the broken tablets
entries.summary: While Moses is on the mountain, the people ask Aaron for gods to go before them. The calf, the broken tablets, and Moses’s intercession expose how quickly a rescued people can turn aside. Kings later describes Jeroboam’s calves at Bethel and Dan, giving readers a powerful textual comparison across centuries.
entries.date: Exodus chronology and routes debated

entries.title: A dwelling in the wilderness
entries.summary: The sanctuary is made to travel with the people. Artisans, materials, the ark, and ordered service occupy much of the latter part of Exodus, ending with the cloud and glory filling the dwelling. Follow the ark forward to Shiloh and Jerusalem to see how the story of divine presence intersects with the story of kings.
entries.date: Exodus chronology and routes debated

entries.title: At the edge of the land
entries.summary: The scouts return with fruit and conflicting judgments. Caleb and Joshua urge trust, while the community recoils in fear. The ensuing wilderness years shape the transition between generations. The reference to Anak’s descendants connects this account with later encounters in the land, without identifying every biblical giant tradition as the same story.
entries.date: Exodus chronology and routes debated

entries.title: A challenge in the camp
entries.summary: Korah, Dathan, and Abiram challenge the leadership of Moses and Aaron. Numbers presents the conflict as a dispute over authority and holiness, followed by judgment and renewed instruction concerning priestly service. The community’s internal fractures are as important to the wilderness story as its external enemies.
entries.date: Exodus chronology and routes debated

entries.title: A hired curse becomes a blessing
entries.summary: Balak of Moab summons Balaam to curse Israel. The journey includes the startling episode of the speaking donkey; the speeches repeatedly turn toward blessing instead. Later passages remember Balaam critically. Reading those texts together prevents a single dramatic episode from becoming the whole account of this complicated figure.
entries.date: Exodus chronology and routes debated

entries.title: A view from Nebo
entries.summary: Moses addresses a new generation in Deuteronomy, then views the land from Nebo before his death. Joshua receives the task of leading onward. The transition joins memory, covenant, and unfinished hope: the one who leads the people out of Egypt does not lead them across the Jordan.
entries.date: Exodus chronology and routes debated

entries.title: Across the Jordan
entries.summary: The ark goes before the people as they cross the Jordan. Memorial stones are set up so future children can ask what happened here. Joshua’s opening movement deliberately recalls the sea crossing, connecting a new generation with the story of deliverance from Egypt.
entries.date: Narrative sequence · overlapping generations

entries.title: Jericho and Rahab
entries.summary: Rahab shelters the spies and asks that her household be spared. Joshua’s account then describes the circling of Jericho and the fall of its walls. The same city contains a story of rescue and a difficult account of destruction. The atlas follows the narrative without claiming that archaeological questions about its dating are settled.
entries.date: Narrative sequence · overlapping generations

entries.title: Choose whom you will serve
entries.summary: Near the end of Joshua’s story, the people gather at Shechem. The address reaches back to Abraham’s family beyond the river, tying the present generation to the ancestral call. Joseph’s bones are also buried at Shechem. Place, memory, covenant, and a long-delayed family promise meet here.
entries.date: Narrative sequence · overlapping generations

entries.title: Deborah, Barak, and a song
entries.summary: Deborah serves as prophet and judge. She summons Barak, and the story of conflict with Sisera culminates in Jael’s action and a victory song. Judges 4 and 5 tell the episode in prose and poetry. Reading both lets us hear the same deliverance through different literary voices.
entries.date: Narrative sequence · overlapping generations

entries.title: Gideon and the reduced army
entries.summary: Called while threshing in fear, Gideon becomes the leader of a force deliberately reduced before battle with Midian. The aftermath complicates the victory: an ephod becomes a snare, and his family’s story turns toward Abimelech’s violence. Judges asks us to look beyond the exciting battle to the consequences of leadership.
entries.date: Narrative sequence · overlapping generations

entries.title: Jephthah’s terrible vow
entries.summary: An excluded son becomes a military leader, but his vow brings devastation into his own household. Judges leaves a deeply troubling story about victory, speech, and a daughter whose future is taken from her. Interpretations differ over the precise fulfillment of the vow; the reader can examine the passage rather than having that debate silently resolved for them.
entries.date: Narrative sequence · overlapping generations

entries.title: Strength and captivity
entries.summary: Samson’s extraordinary strength unfolds alongside impulsive choices and conflict with the Philistines. Delilah’s betrayal leads to imprisonment in Gaza; the final scene brings destruction upon both Samson and his captors. His story closes without the uncomplicated peace a reader might expect from a deliverer.
entries.date: Narrative sequence · overlapping generations

entries.title: Ruth chooses to stay
entries.summary: A famine, bereavement, and the journey from Moab bring Ruth and Naomi to Bethlehem. Ruth’s loyalty and Boaz’s protection lead to a new household. The book ends with a genealogy: Ruth becomes the great-grandmother of David. A story of gleaning and family care stands inside the story of a kingdom.
entries.date: Narrative sequence · overlapping generations

entries.title: A prayer at Shiloh
entries.summary: Hannah brings her grief to the sanctuary at Shiloh. Samuel’s birth and dedication lead into a song about reversals: strength and weakness, hunger and fullness, humiliation and honor. Her family story opens the book that will trace Israel’s transition to monarchy.
entries.date: Narrative sequence · overlapping generations

entries.title: The ark leaves Shiloh’s world
entries.summary: Israel takes the ark into battle, but the army is defeated and the ark captured. The Philistine episodes that follow overturn the assumption that possessing a sacred object means controlling its power. The ark’s later journey to Jerusalem will carry the memory of these events.
entries.date: Narrative sequence · overlapping generations

entries.title: Samuel and the demand for a king
entries.summary: Called as a child in Eli’s household, Samuel becomes a prophet and judge during a changing political world. When the people demand a king, he warns about royal power and then participates in the anointing of Saul and David. He connects the age of judges with the monarchy.
entries.date: Narrative sequence · overlapping generations

entries.title: David in the Valley of Elah
entries.summary: A shepherd enters a military standoff and confronts Goliath with a sling. The chapter contrasts armor, reputation, and confidence in God. It also introduces the public consequences of David’s courage: his place in Saul’s household and his growing reputation become central to the conflict that follows.
entries.date: Conventionally c. 1050–931 BCE

entries.title: The fall of Saul’s house
entries.summary: The battle on Gilboa brings the deaths of Saul and Jonathan. David’s lament refuses to reduce their deaths to political convenience. The transition is not immediate or uncontested: Saul’s son Ish-bosheth also rules before David becomes king over all Israel.
entries.date: Conventionally c. 1050–931 BCE

entries.title: David takes Jerusalem
entries.summary: David first rules from Hebron. After the tribes recognize him, Jerusalem becomes his capital. The city’s political importance grows alongside its religious importance, binding the royal household and the future temple to the same place.
entries.date: Conventionally c. 1050–931 BCE

entries.title: The ark comes to Jerusalem
entries.summary: Bringing the ark to Jerusalem involves celebration, death, fear, and a renewed attempt. David dances, while Michal’s response exposes tension inside the royal household. The story connects the portable sanctuary of Exodus with the city that will become the center of temple worship.
entries.date: Conventionally c. 1050–931 BCE

entries.title: A house and a promise
entries.summary: David wants to build a house for God, but Nathan delivers a promise about David’s own house—his dynasty. The passage links kingship, succession, discipline, and enduring mercy. It becomes an important thread for understanding both royal hope and the crisis of exile.
entries.date: Conventionally c. 1050–931 BCE

entries.title: Nathan confronts the king
entries.summary: David takes Bathsheba and arranges the death of her husband Uriah. Nathan’s parable exposes the king’s wrongdoing. The account refuses to shield a celebrated king from moral judgment, and the consequences move through the subsequent history of David’s household.
entries.date: Conventionally c. 1050–931 BCE

entries.title: A son’s revolt
entries.summary: Absalom’s story emerges from violence and failed justice within David’s family. He wins support, drives David from Jerusalem, and dies during the ensuing conflict. David’s grief makes the political struggle painfully personal: the rival claimant is still his son.
entries.date: Conventionally c. 1050–931 BCE

entries.title: Solomon’s temple
entries.summary: The temple draws together royal ambition, skilled labor, international cooperation, and worship. Solomon’s dedication asks whether God can truly be contained in a building and includes prayer for a future people in exile. Read that prayer beside the temple’s destruction to see how Kings connects its beginning and ending.
entries.date: Conventionally c. 1050–931 BCE

entries.title: A queen comes with questions
entries.summary: The queen of Sheba comes to test Solomon with difficult questions and sees his wisdom and royal splendor. Kings and Chronicles tell this visit briefly. The later Ethiopian Kebra Nagast develops a much larger account; it is a distinct work, not a chapter of Kings or a book that this atlas silently folds into the biblical canon.
entries.date: Conventionally c. 1050–931 BCE
entries.note: The identification of Sheba and the later Ethiopian royal tradition deserve separate treatment. The visitor’s personal name is not given in Kings.

entries.title: One kingdom becomes two
entries.summary: At Shechem, Rehoboam refuses the request to ease the burden imposed under Solomon. The northern tribes turn to Jeroboam, while Rehoboam retains Judah. From here, the reader has to follow two royal histories at once. The kings view makes that parallel story visible.
entries.date: Conventionally c. 931 BCE

entries.title: Ahijah’s torn cloak
entries.summary: Ahijah of Shiloh meets Jeroboam and tears a new garment into twelve pieces, giving him ten. The symbolic act announces a division of Solomon’s kingdom while also placing conditions on Jeroboam’s rule. Later, the same prophet brings judgment on Jeroboam’s household.
entries.date: Conventionally c. 931–722 BCE

entries.title: Elijah enters the story
entries.summary: Elijah announces drought in Ahab’s reign, is sustained in unexpected places, and encounters a widow at Zarephath. His ministry confronts royal power and competing worship, but also includes exhaustion and the need for renewal. He belongs in the same historical view as Ahab, Jezebel, and Jehoshaphat.
entries.date: Ninth century BCE; ministries not precisely dated

entries.title: The confrontation on Carmel
entries.summary: Elijah gathers the people on Carmel and challenges their divided allegiance. The contest with the prophets of Baal leads to fire, judgment, and rain after drought. The following chapter’s flight and despair are part of the same prophet’s story; the mountaintop victory is not the end of it.
entries.date: Conventionally c. 931–722 BCE

entries.title: A vineyard and a king’s appetite
entries.summary: Naboth refuses to surrender his ancestral inheritance to Ahab. Jezebel arranges accusations and his death, after which Ahab takes the vineyard. Elijah confronts the king. This story connects land, inheritance, false testimony, and royal abuse of power in a single household’s loss.
entries.date: Conventionally c. 931–722 BCE

entries.title: Two kings at Ramoth-gilead
entries.summary: Ahab of Israel and Jehoshaphat of Judah join in battle against Aram. Micaiah’s warning stands against the favorable message of the other prophets. Ahab goes disguised, is struck by an arrow, and dies. This is a clear point where the histories of the two kingdoms meet.
entries.date: Conventionally c. 853 BCE

entries.title: Micaiah refuses the easy answer
entries.summary: Asked to join the reassuring voices before battle, Micaiah insists on speaking what he is given. His vision of the heavenly council and his warning about the scattered people form the theological center of the Ramoth-gilead episode. His message is rejected, but Kings then narrates Ahab’s death.
entries.date: Conventionally c. 931–722 BCE

entries.title: Elisha takes up the mantle
entries.summary: Elisha follows Elijah and receives his mantle after the departure at the Jordan. His stories move through households, famine, healing, war, and royal succession. The succession is prophetic, not a father-to-son dynasty; the family view does not turn it into one.
entries.date: Conventionally c. 931–722 BCE

entries.title: A commander washes in the Jordan
entries.summary: An unnamed captive girl points Naaman, an Aramean commander, toward help in Israel. Elisha’s instructions disappoint him, but his servants persuade him to wash in the Jordan. Healing crosses the boundary between rival peoples, and the chapter ends by turning its scrutiny toward Gehazi’s greed.
entries.date: Conventionally c. 931–722 BCE

entries.title: The house of Ahab falls
entries.summary: An anointing sets Jehu’s revolt in motion. Joram of Israel, Ahaziah of Judah, and Jezebel die as the coup unfolds, followed by the destruction of Ahab’s house. Kings and Hosea do not offer a simple, identical appraisal of the violence. Their different emphases should remain visible.
entries.date: Conventionally c. 841 BCE

entries.title: Jonah and the enemy city
entries.summary: The book of Jonah tells of flight, a great fish, a commission to Nineveh, and a prophet angry at mercy. Separately, 2 Kings 14 names Jonah son of Amittai in the time of Jeroboam II. The narrative’s Assyrian king is unnamed, so this atlas does not assign the Nineveh episode an exact year.
entries.date: Conventionally c. 931–722 BCE
entries.note: The time of Jonah’s ministry, the setting of the narrative, and the book’s composition are separate questions.

entries.title: Justice at the royal sanctuary
entries.summary: Amos speaks against exploitation, complacency, and worship detached from justice. The book places his words in the reigns of Uzziah of Judah and Jeroboam II of Israel. His confrontation with Amaziah at Bethel lets us watch a prophet challenge the assumptions of a royal sanctuary.
entries.date: Conventionally c. 931–722 BCE

entries.title: Covenant and unfaithfulness
entries.summary: Hosea’s family imagery and prophetic speeches expose the northern kingdom’s unfaithfulness while returning again to divine compassion. Its opening names kings in both Judah and Israel. The book’s mention of the bloodshed at Jezreel invites comparison with the account of Jehu in Kings.
entries.date: Conventionally c. 931–722 BCE

entries.title: A vision and a kingdom in danger
entries.summary: Isaiah’s call is set in the year of Uzziah’s death. His ministry intersects the reigns of Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah as Assyrian power grows. The book connects the holiness of God with the public life of a threatened kingdom. Its later chapters also speak into exile and hope; they are not all pinned to one moment.
entries.date: Conventionally c. 931–722 BCE

entries.title: What does the Lord require?
entries.summary: Micah addresses Samaria and Jerusalem during the reigns named in his opening: Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah. His words move from judgment against predatory power to hope for restoration. Jeremiah later remembers Micah’s warning as an example of prophetic speech heard in Hezekiah’s time.
entries.date: Conventionally c. 931–722 BCE

entries.title: The northern kingdom falls
entries.summary: The Assyrian siege of Samaria ends the northern monarchy. 2 Kings 17 recounts Hoshea’s rebellion and the fall, then offers a long theological explanation of exile. The population movements that follow change the land’s political and religious landscape. Judah continues, but the two-kingdom story is no longer symmetrical.

entries.title: Jerusalem under threat
entries.summary: After the fall of the northern kingdom, Sennacherib’s forces threaten Judah. Lachish and Jerusalem become centers of the crisis, while Isaiah addresses Hezekiah. Kings, Isaiah, and Chronicles preserve accounts with different emphases. Assyrian evidence also records the campaign; the atlas’s date is the conventional 701 BCE anchor.
entries.date: 701 BCE

entries.title: Manasseh and the possibility of return
entries.summary: Kings emphasizes Manasseh’s wrongdoing and its consequences. Chronicles also tells of his captivity, humbling, and return. The Prayer of Manasseh gives voice to repentance in a distinct transmitted prayer; it should not be presented as a quotation found inside Kings. Reading these sources together reveals their different portraits.
entries.note: The Prayer of Manasseh is a separate work associated with the king, not a passage embedded in 2 Kings.

entries.title: A scroll is found
entries.summary: During repairs to the temple, a book of the law is found and read to Josiah. Huldah interprets the situation, and the king leads a public covenant renewal and reform. The narrative joins a recovered text with renewed responsibility; hearing and responding are inseparable.
entries.date: Josiah’s eighteenth year; conventionally c. 622 BCE

entries.title: The prophet consulted by the king
entries.summary: When Josiah’s officials seek a word about the discovered scroll, they go to Huldah in Jerusalem. Her answer combines judgment on the kingdom with a word concerning the king’s response. She belongs at the center of this episode of reform, not at its margins.

entries.title: The fall of Nineveh envisioned
entries.summary: Nahum addresses Nineveh with language of judgment against a violent imperial power. Read alongside Jonah, the same city becomes a place where different prophetic books explore mercy, repentance, oppression, and judgment. The precise date of Nahum’s ministry is uncertain; Nineveh’s historical fall is conventionally dated to 612 BCE.
entries.note: A prophet’s oracle is not automatically a dated eyewitness report of the city’s fall.

entries.title: A warning in Josiah’s reign
entries.summary: Zephaniah’s opening places his prophecy in the reign of Josiah. Judgment reaches Judah and surrounding peoples, but the book also speaks of a humble remnant and restoration. Its royal setting is explicit even though the exact years of the prophet’s ministry are not.

entries.title: Josiah meets Pharaoh Neco
entries.summary: Josiah’s reign ends when he meets Pharaoh Neco at Megiddo. Kings gives a brief account; Chronicles adds a fuller scene and a warning Josiah does not heed. His death changes the political situation of Judah as Egypt and Babylon struggle for influence.
entries.date: 609 BCE

entries.title: A prophet through the collapse
entries.summary: Jeremiah’s ministry begins in Josiah’s time and continues into the catastrophe of Jerusalem. His messages confront false reassurance, injustice, and the temptation to treat the temple as a guarantee. The book also preserves promises of restoration and a new covenant amid judgment.

entries.title: How long?
entries.summary: Habakkuk argues with God about violence and the rise of the Chaldeans. The book does not name a reigning Judahite king, so its location near the Babylonian crisis is a broad setting rather than a precise date. Complaint, waiting, and trust belong together in this prophetic conversation.
entries.note: Placed broadly near the rise of Babylon; the book itself does not provide a regnal date.

entries.title: A king carried to Babylon
entries.summary: Jehoiachin’s surrender is followed by deportation of royal officials, warriors, craftspeople, and treasures. Nebuchadnezzar installs Zedekiah. The story does not end with this first capture: a further rebellion and a more devastating siege lie ahead. Ezekiel’s prophetic setting is among the exiles.
entries.date: 597 BCE

entries.title: Visions among the exiles
entries.summary: Ezekiel’s opening vision is set among the exiles by the river Chebar, in the fifth year of Jehoiachin’s exile. His enacted signs, visions, and promises of restoration address people far from Jerusalem. The precise Chebar location is not mapped here; the Babylon marker provides regional orientation.

entries.title: Jerusalem and the temple burn
entries.summary: Zedekiah’s rebellion leads to siege, famine, capture, and the destruction of Jerusalem’s temple. The objects, buildings, and royal hopes that occupied earlier chapters of Kings are dismantled. Jeremiah 52 offers a parallel account. The event is commonly dated to 587 or 586 BCE; the atlas uses the latter as its display convention.
entries.date: 587/586 BCE (display: 586)

entries.title: A fragile life after the siege
entries.summary: Gedaliah is appointed over the people remaining in Judah and is based at Mizpah. His assassination destroys a fragile attempt at stability, and fear leads survivors toward Egypt. The aftermath of a city’s fall is its own human story, not simply the empty space after a royal timeline ends.

entries.title: A seat at the king’s table
entries.summary: Kings ends with an unexpected change of scene. Jehoiachin is released from prison in Babylon and receives provision at the royal table. The land and temple have not been restored, but the narrative leaves a surviving member of David’s house alive. It is an ending that invites the reader to keep following the promise.

entries.title: Adam
entries.summary: The first human in the garden account and the starting point of the genealogy traced through Seth to Noah. Genesis 4 also preserves a separate line through Cain.
entries.date: Story order · no assigned BCE dates

entries.title: Eve
entries.summary: Named as the mother of all living in Genesis, Eve belongs to both the garden story and the painful family story that follows it.
entries.date: Story order · no assigned BCE dates

entries.title: Seth
entries.summary: A son of Adam and Eve, named after Abel’s death; the genealogy of Genesis 5 continues through his line.
entries.date: Story order · no assigned BCE dates

entries.title: Enosh
entries.summary: Son of Seth and father of Kenan in the genealogy of Genesis 5.
entries.date: Story order · no assigned BCE dates

entries.title: Kenan
entries.summary: Son of Enosh and father of Mahalalel in the Genesis 5 genealogy.
entries.date: Story order · no assigned BCE dates

entries.title: Mahalalel
entries.summary: Son of Kenan and father of Jared in the Genesis 5 genealogy.
entries.date: Story order · no assigned BCE dates

entries.title: Jared
entries.summary: Father of Enoch. 1 Enoch 6 places the descent of the Watchers in the days of Jared.
entries.date: Story order · no assigned BCE dates

entries.title: Methuselah
entries.summary: Son of Enoch and father of Lamech; in 1 Enoch 106 he seeks an explanation of Noah’s extraordinary birth.
entries.date: Story order · no assigned BCE dates

entries.title: Lamech, Noah’s father
entries.summary: Noah’s father in Seth’s line. He must not be confused with the Lamech in Cain’s genealogy in Genesis 4.
entries.date: Story order · no assigned BCE dates

entries.title: Shem
entries.summary: A son of Noah; the genealogical line toward Terah and Abraham is traced through Shem.
entries.date: Story order · no assigned BCE dates

entries.title: Ham
entries.summary: A son of Noah named in the post-Flood family stories and the table of nations.
entries.date: Story order · no assigned BCE dates

entries.title: Japheth
entries.summary: A son of Noah whose descendants appear in the table of nations.
entries.date: Story order · no assigned BCE dates

entries.title: Terah
entries.summary: Father of Abram, Nahor, and Haran. Genesis describes the household moving from Ur toward Canaan and settling in Haran.
entries.date: Ancestral narratives · dates debated

entries.title: Abraham / Abram
entries.summary: Called out of his homeland, Abraham receives promises of descendants, land, and blessing. His story includes courage, hospitality, uncertainty, and failures; Genesis and Jubilees supply related but distinct accounts.
entries.date: Ancestral narratives · dates debated

entries.title: Sarah / Sarai
entries.summary: Abraham’s wife and Isaac’s mother. Her story carries the long wait for a child, laughter at an extraordinary promise, and conflict concerning Hagar and Ishmael.
entries.date: Ancestral narratives · dates debated

entries.title: Hagar
entries.summary: An Egyptian woman in Sarah’s household and the mother of Ishmael. Her encounters in the wilderness give a powerful place to a person at risk of being overlooked within the ancestral story.
entries.date: Ancestral narratives · dates debated

entries.title: Ishmael
entries.summary: Son of Abraham and Hagar. Genesis gives him a promise of descendants and preserves his genealogy alongside the line through Isaac.
entries.date: Ancestral narratives · dates debated

entries.title: Isaac
entries.summary: Son of Abraham and Sarah, husband of Rebekah, and father of Esau and Jacob. His story includes the test on the mountain and the struggle over the family blessing.
entries.date: Ancestral narratives · dates debated

entries.title: Rebekah
entries.summary: Wife of Isaac and mother of Esau and Jacob. Her decisive actions connect the marriage story of Genesis 24 with the contested blessing in Genesis 27.
entries.date: Ancestral narratives · dates debated

entries.title: Lot
entries.summary: Son of Haran and nephew of Abraham. His separation from Abraham and life near Sodom connect the ancestral family with the cities of the plain.
entries.date: Ancestral narratives · dates debated

entries.title: Esau / Edom
entries.summary: Isaac and Rebekah’s elder son, Jacob’s twin. Conflict over birthright and blessing eventually gives way to a meeting marked by fear and reconciliation.
entries.date: Ancestral narratives · dates debated

entries.title: Jacob / Israel
entries.summary: Son of Isaac and Rebekah. The ancestral story follows him through deception, exile, marriages, wrestling, reconciliation, and grief before the family’s move to Egypt.
entries.date: Ancestral narratives · dates debated

entries.title: Leah
entries.summary: Daughter of Laban and wife of Jacob. Genesis names six sons and Dinah among her children; Judah’s and Levi’s lines become particularly important later.
entries.date: Ancestral narratives · dates debated

entries.title: Rachel
entries.summary: Daughter of Laban, wife of Jacob, and mother of Joseph and Benjamin. Her long desire for children and death after Benjamin’s birth shape the family’s story.
entries.date: Ancestral narratives · dates debated

entries.title: Bilhah
entries.summary: Rachel’s servant, given to Jacob; mother of Dan and Naphtali in Genesis’s account of the household.
entries.date: Ancestral narratives · dates debated

entries.title: Zilpah
entries.summary: Leah’s servant, given to Jacob; mother of Gad and Asher.
entries.date: Ancestral narratives · dates debated

entries.title: Joseph
entries.summary: Son of Jacob and Rachel. Sold into Egypt, imprisoned, and elevated to authority, he becomes the means of preserving his family during famine.
entries.date: Ancestral narratives · dates debated

entries.title: Reuben
entries.summary: Firstborn son of Jacob and Leah; his place in the household is revisited in Jacob’s final words.
entries.date: Ancestral narratives · dates debated

entries.title: Simeon
entries.summary: Son of Jacob and Leah, paired with Levi in the violent aftermath of the assault on Dinah.
entries.date: Ancestral narratives · dates debated

entries.title: Levi
entries.summary: Son of Jacob and Leah. The family line of Moses, Aaron, and Miriam is traced through Levi.
entries.date: Ancestral narratives · dates debated

entries.title: Judah
entries.summary: Son of Jacob and Leah. His story connects the brothers’ betrayal of Joseph, Tamar, and the later ancestry of David.
entries.date: Ancestral narratives · dates debated

entries.title: Issachar
entries.summary: A son of Jacob and Leah, named in the family list that underlies the tribal traditions.
entries.date: Ancestral narratives · dates debated

entries.title: Zebulun
entries.summary: A son of Jacob and Leah, named in the family list that underlies the tribal traditions.
entries.date: Ancestral narratives · dates debated

entries.title: Dinah
entries.summary: Daughter of Jacob and Leah. Genesis 34 tells of the violence against her and the destructive response of her brothers.
entries.date: Ancestral narratives · dates debated

entries.title: Dan
entries.summary: Son of Jacob and Bilhah; the name is also used for a tribe and, later, a northern city.
entries.date: Ancestral narratives · dates debated

entries.title: Naphtali
entries.summary: Son of Jacob and Bilhah, an ancestor named in the tribal traditions.
entries.date: Ancestral narratives · dates debated

entries.title: Gad
entries.summary: Son of Jacob and Zilpah, an ancestor named in the tribal traditions.
entries.date: Ancestral narratives · dates debated

entries.title: Asher
entries.summary: Son of Jacob and Zilpah, an ancestor named in the tribal traditions.
entries.date: Ancestral narratives · dates debated

entries.title: Benjamin
entries.summary: Son of Jacob and Rachel. His mother dies after his birth; his safety later becomes central to Joseph’s testing of the brothers.
entries.date: Ancestral narratives · dates debated

entries.title: Tamar
entries.summary: The woman who challenges Judah’s failure to provide for her future. She becomes the mother of Perez and Zerah.
entries.date: Ancestral narratives · dates debated

entries.title: Perez
entries.summary: Son of Judah and Tamar. Ruth 4 traces the family line from Perez to David.
entries.date: Ancestral narratives · dates debated

entries.title: Moses
entries.summary: Born under an oppressive decree, raised in Pharaoh’s household, and called in the wilderness, Moses becomes the leader of the Exodus and mediator of the covenant. Jubilees frames its revelation as given to him at Sinai.
entries.date: Exodus chronology and routes debated

entries.title: Aaron
entries.summary: Moses’s brother and spokesman, later central to the priestly service. His story includes both consecration and responsibility in the golden-calf episode.
entries.date: Exodus chronology and routes debated

entries.title: Miriam
entries.summary: A prophet associated with the song after the sea crossing and named alongside Moses and Aaron in Israel’s memory of deliverance. Numbers also preserves her conflict with Moses.
entries.date: Exodus chronology and routes debated

entries.title: Joshua
entries.summary: Moses’s successor leads the people across the Jordan and is central to the narratives of entry, allotment, and covenant renewal in the land.
entries.date: Narrative sequence · overlapping generations

entries.title: Rahab
entries.summary: A woman of Jericho who shelters the spies and asks protection for her family. Joshua describes her household’s rescue when the city falls.
entries.date: Narrative sequence · overlapping generations

entries.title: Naomi
entries.summary: Widowed in Moab, Naomi returns to Bethlehem with Ruth. Her movement from loss toward a renewed household shapes the book of Ruth.
entries.date: Narrative sequence · overlapping generations

entries.title: Boaz
entries.summary: A relative of Naomi’s husband and a landowner at Bethlehem. His protection of Ruth and public act of family redemption connect everyday generosity with David’s ancestry.
entries.date: Narrative sequence · overlapping generations

entries.title: Obed
entries.summary: Son of Ruth and Boaz, father of Jesse, and grandfather of David according to Ruth’s closing genealogy.
entries.date: Narrative sequence · overlapping generations

entries.title: Jesse
entries.summary: Father of David, living at Bethlehem when Samuel comes to anoint a king.
entries.date: Conventionally c. 1050–931 BCE

entries.title: Jonathan
entries.summary: Son of Saul and close friend of David. His loyalty to David exists alongside his place in Saul’s royal household; he dies with Saul at Gilboa.
entries.date: Conventionally c. 1050–931 BCE

entries.title: Michal
entries.summary: Saul’s daughter and David’s wife. She helps David escape Saul, and later confronts him after the ark’s entry into Jerusalem.
entries.date: Conventionally c. 1050–931 BCE

entries.title: Ish-bosheth
entries.summary: Saul’s son who is made king by Abner after Saul’s death. His rule overlaps David’s early reign at Hebron; the atlas does not pretend the transition was uncontested.
entries.date: Conventionally c. 1050–931 BCE

entries.title: Bathsheba
entries.summary: Wife of Uriah, later David’s wife and Solomon’s mother. Her story belongs both to David’s grave wrongdoing and to the struggle over royal succession.
entries.date: Conventionally c. 1050–931 BCE

entries.title: Nathan speaks to David
entries.summary: Nathan delivers the promise concerning David’s house, confronts David after the death of Uriah, and acts during the dispute over Solomon’s succession. His role shows a prophet speaking both promise and correction to the same king.
entries.date: Conventionally c. 1050–931 BCE

entries.title: Jezebel
entries.summary: Daughter of Ethbaal, king of the Sidonians, and wife of Ahab. Kings connects her with persecution of prophets, the death of Naboth, and the violent fall of Ahab’s house.
entries.date: Conventionally c. 931–722 BCE

entries.title: Saul
entries.summary: Israel’s first king in Samuel’s narrative. His story moves from anointing and military success to disobedience, conflict with David, and death at Gilboa.
entries.note: These early-monarchy dates are broad conventional estimates, not a settled archaeological chronology.

entries.title: David
entries.summary: Shepherd, fugitive, and king. David makes Jerusalem his capital and receives a dynastic promise, but the books of Samuel also preserve his serious failures and the suffering within his household.
entries.note: These early-monarchy dates are broad conventional estimates, not a settled archaeological chronology.

entries.title: Solomon
entries.summary: David and Bathsheba’s son, associated with wisdom and the temple. Kings also describes burdensome rule and divided loyalties that prepare the way for the kingdom’s fracture.
entries.note: These early-monarchy dates are broad conventional estimates, not a settled archaeological chronology.

entries.title: Jeroboam I
entries.summary: The first king of the northern kingdom. His sanctuaries at Bethel and Dan become a repeated point of judgment in the books of Kings.

entries.title: Nadab
entries.summary: Jeroboam’s son. Baasha kills him during a siege and brings Jeroboam’s royal house to an end.

entries.title: Baasha
entries.summary: His coup ends Jeroboam’s dynasty, but Kings judges his own rule by the same pattern of wrongdoing. He also conflicts with Asa of Judah.

entries.title: Elah
entries.summary: Baasha’s son, killed by Zimri while drinking at Tirzah. His short reign ends another northern dynasty.

entries.title: Zimri
entries.summary: His coup is followed by only seven days of rule at Tirzah. The army makes Omri king, and Zimri dies when the palace burns.
entries.date: c. 885 BCE · short reign

entries.title: Tibni, rival claimant
entries.summary: A portion of the people supports Tibni while another supports Omri. He is shown as a rival claimant, not as an uncontested successor between Zimri and Omri.

entries.title: Omri
entries.summary: After civil conflict, Omri establishes his rule and builds Samaria as the northern capital. His dynasty continues through Ahab.

entries.title: Ahab
entries.summary: Son of Omri and husband of Jezebel. Elijah’s confrontations, Naboth’s vineyard, and the alliance with Jehoshaphat all meet within his reign.

entries.title: Ahaziah of Israel
entries.summary: Ahab’s son. His appeal to Baal-zebub after an injury brings a confrontation with Elijah. Do not confuse him with the later Ahaziah of Judah.

entries.title: Joram / Jehoram of Israel
entries.summary: Ahab’s son, ruling during Elisha’s ministry. His alliance with Ahaziah of Judah ends in Jehu’s revolt. Another Jehoram rules Judah during part of the same era.

entries.title: Jehu
entries.summary: An anointed commander whose revolt destroys Ahab’s house. Compare Kings’s account with Hosea’s later reference to the bloodshed of Jezreel.

entries.title: Jehoahaz of Israel
entries.summary: Jehu’s son, whose kingdom suffers under Aramean pressure. Kings describes both his appeal for help and the continuing religious failures of the kingdom.

entries.title: Jehoash / Joash of Israel
entries.summary: He visits the dying Elisha and later defeats Amaziah of Judah. His name is easily confused with Joash of Judah, so the atlas always supplies the kingdom.

entries.title: Jeroboam II
entries.summary: A period of northern expansion, also the royal setting named by Amos and Hosea. Kings connects a prophecy of Jonah son of Amittai with the restoration of territory.

entries.title: Zechariah of Israel
entries.summary: Jeroboam II’s son, ruling for six months before Shallum’s coup. His death ends Jehu’s dynasty. This is not the later prophet Zechariah.
entries.date: c. 753 BCE · short reign

entries.title: Shallum
entries.summary: His coup gives him a month of rule in Samaria before Menahem kills him. Short reigns are shown as small markers rather than fabricated full-year reigns.
entries.date: c. 752 BCE · short reign

entries.title: Menahem
entries.summary: He takes the throne by violence and pays tribute to the Assyrian king Pul to strengthen his rule. Northern politics are increasingly entangled with imperial power.

entries.title: Pekahiah
entries.summary: Menahem’s son, killed by Pekah in a palace conspiracy at Samaria.

entries.title: Pekah
entries.summary: He joins Rezin of Aram against Judah while Assyria takes northern territory. His reported twenty years require chronological reconstruction; this display uses the comparison table’s sole-rule convention.

entries.title: Hoshea
entries.summary: The northern kingdom’s last king. Rebellion against Assyria leads to imprisonment and the siege of Samaria.

entries.title: Rehoboam
entries.summary: Solomon’s son. His answer to the request for relief precipitates the split, and his reign faces invasion by Shishak of Egypt.

entries.title: Abijah / Abijam
entries.summary: Rehoboam’s son. Kings and Chronicles give different amounts of attention to his short reign and the conflict with the north.

entries.title: Asa
entries.summary: A reforming king who removes idols, yet later turns to an alliance with Aram against Baasha. Chronicles preserves prophetic criticism of that choice.

entries.title: Jehoshaphat
entries.summary: He rules Judah alongside Ahab in Israel and joins him at Ramoth-gilead. Chronicles expands the portrait with teaching, reform, and further alliances.

entries.title: Jehoram of Judah
entries.summary: Jehoshaphat’s son, married into Ahab’s house. Kings connects his reign with Edom’s revolt. He is distinct from the contemporary Joram of Israel.

entries.title: Ahaziah of Judah
entries.summary: Son of Jehoram and Athaliah. He joins Joram of Israel and is caught in Jehu’s revolt. His short reign creates a succession crisis in Judah.
entries.date: c. 841 BCE · short reign

entries.title: Athaliah
entries.summary: After her son Ahaziah’s death, Athaliah seizes power. Joash is hidden, and a later alliance around the priest Jehoiada brings her rule to an end. Her exact placement within Omri’s family is described with different kinship wording in Kings.

entries.title: Joash / Jehoash of Judah
entries.summary: Hidden as a child, crowned after Athaliah’s overthrow, and associated with temple repairs. Chronicles tells a darker later story after Jehoiada’s death.

entries.title: Amaziah
entries.summary: Son of Joash. After victory over Edom, he challenges Jehoash of Israel and suffers defeat and the plundering of Jerusalem.

entries.title: Uzziah / Azariah
entries.summary: A long reign associated with strength and a later affliction. The year of his death provides the setting of Isaiah’s throne vision. Co-regencies affect attempts to reconstruct the full chronology.

entries.title: Jotham
entries.summary: Son of Uzziah, active in leadership during his father’s affliction and then king. His era is named in the openings of Isaiah and Micah.

entries.title: Ahaz
entries.summary: Facing Israel and Aram, Ahaz turns to Assyria for help. Isaiah’s encounter with him belongs to this political crisis.

entries.title: Hezekiah
entries.summary: A reforming king who faces Sennacherib’s invasion. Isaiah, the threatened city, and later Babylonian visitors connect his reign with both deliverance and the shadow of exile.

entries.title: Manasseh
entries.summary: Kings emphasizes wrongdoing and its long consequences; Chronicles adds captivity and repentance. The separately transmitted Prayer of Manasseh belongs to the wider reading tradition.

entries.title: Amon
entries.summary: Manasseh’s son, killed by palace officials after a short reign. The people then make his son Josiah king.

entries.title: Josiah
entries.summary: The discovery of a law book, Huldah’s message, covenant renewal, and Passover mark a major reform. His death at Megiddo opens Judah’s final unstable decades.

entries.title: Jehoahaz of Judah
entries.summary: Josiah’s son, chosen after his father’s death but deposed by Pharaoh Neco after three months and taken to Egypt.
entries.date: c. 609 BCE · short reign

entries.title: Jehoiakim
entries.summary: Installed by Neco, he later becomes entangled with Babylon. Jeremiah 36 describes his destruction of a prophetic scroll.

entries.title: Jehoiachin / Jeconiah
entries.summary: He surrenders during the Babylonian capture and is taken into exile. His later release supplies the final scene of Kings.

entries.title: Zedekiah
entries.summary: Installed by Babylon, he rebels and rules through Jerusalem’s final siege. He is Josiah’s son and Jehoiachin’s uncle, not Jehoiachin’s son.

entries.title: Faithfulness in a foreign court
entries.summary: Daniel and his companions are given new names and a place in Babylon’s royal training. They cannot choose the empire around them, but they can choose faithfulness within it. The exile becomes the setting of a story about wisdom, courage, and a kingdom no human ruler can finally own.
entries.date: Exile and Persian-period settings · some stories overlap era 07
entries.note: Daniel’s narrative setting and the book’s composition are separate historical questions.

entries.title: A fourth figure in the fire
entries.summary: Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego refuse to bow before the king’s golden image. Their answer does not bargain for a rescue: God can deliver them, but even if He does not, they will not worship the image. In the furnace, the king sees a fourth figure; the story turns imperial spectacle into testimony.
entries.date: Exile and Persian-period settings · some stories overlap era 07
entries.note: The king describes the fourth figure in 3:25; 3:28 calls the deliverer an angel. Identifying that figure specifically as the preincarnate Christ is a Christian interpretation, not an explicit identification in the passage.

entries.title: The writing on the wall
entries.summary: At Belshazzar’s feast, vessels taken from Jerusalem’s temple become drinking cups. A hand writes a judgment that the court cannot read. Daniel interprets the message: power has been weighed, found wanting, and is passing away. The city of exile itself stands under judgment.
entries.date: Exile and Persian-period settings · some stories overlap era 07

entries.title: Prayer when the windows stay open
entries.summary: A royal decree makes Daniel’s ordinary prayer a dangerous act. He continues to pray toward Jerusalem and is thrown into the lions’ den. The king cannot simply undo his own law; deliverance comes from the God Daniel serves. Faithfulness is shown in a daily habit before it becomes a dramatic rescue.
entries.date: Exile and Persian-period settings · some stories overlap era 07
entries.note: The identity of “Darius the Mede” is debated. This entry follows the story without assigning him an uncontested identification or calendar year.

entries.title: One like a son of man
entries.summary: Beastly empires rise from the sea, but Daniel’s vision does not end with the beasts. Before the Ancient of Days, one like a son of man receives an everlasting dominion, and the holy ones receive the kingdom. Jesus’ use of “Son of Man” and Revelation’s throne-room imagery invite readers back into this vision.
entries.date: Exile and Persian-period settings · some stories overlap era 07
entries.note: The vision explains the beasts as kingdoms and connects dominion with the holy ones. Its reception in the Gospels and Revelation is part of the connection, not a claim that every interpretive question has one answer.

entries.title: Can these bones live?
entries.summary: Ezekiel stands before a valley of dry bones and hears a question only God can answer. Bone joins bone; breath enters the slain. The passage itself names the bones as the whole house of Israel, speaking hope to a people who say their hope is lost. Resurrection imagery grows from a concrete promise of restoration.
entries.date: Exile and Persian-period settings · some stories overlap era 07

entries.title: The road home opens
entries.summary: The opening of Ezra announces a change no prisoner could manufacture: Cyrus permits the rebuilding of the house of God in Jerusalem. Families prepare to return, neighbors contribute, and temple vessels come out of imperial storage. The promise surviving at the end of Kings now has a road to travel.
entries.date: Cyrus’s decree conventionally placed c. 538 BCE

entries.title: A foundation laid with tears and joy
entries.summary: Returned exiles rebuild the altar and lay the temple’s foundation. Some shout for joy; those who remember the former house weep. Opposition and discouragement delay the work, but Haggai and Zechariah call the community forward. The rebuilt temple becomes part of the world Jesus will enter.
entries.date: Rebuilding after the return · completion conventionally c. 515 BCE

entries.title: Zerubbabel: a royal line after exile
entries.summary: Zerubbabel leads returned exiles and takes part in rebuilding the temple. Haggai addresses him as governor of Judah, not as a restored king. Matthew later includes him in the genealogy that leads through Joseph’s household to Jesus: exile interrupts the monarchy, but not the Gospel’s tracing of the promise.
entries.date: Exile and Persian-period settings · some stories overlap era 07

entries.title: The Branch, the lampstand & the coming king
entries.summary: Zechariah speaks to a rebuilding community with visions of cleansing, lampstands, and olive trees, and with promises of a figure called the Branch. Elsewhere a humble king arrives on a donkey. These images will reappear in the Gospel accounts of Jesus’ entrance and in Revelation’s witnesses.
entries.date: Exile and Persian-period settings · some stories overlap era 07

entries.title: For such a time as this
entries.summary: In the Persian court at Susa, Esther must decide whether to speak when silence might seem safer. Mordecai’s challenge, a fast, carefully timed banquets, and the exposure of Haman’s plot turn a threat of destruction into deliverance. The story remembers vulnerable people living far from Jerusalem, not only those who returned.
entries.date: Exile and Persian-period settings · some stories overlap era 07
entries.note: This entry follows the Hebrew-form Esther supplied in the reader. The separately supplied Greek additions are not silently blended into it.

entries.title: A broken city becomes a shared task
entries.summary: News of Jerusalem’s broken walls draws prayer from Nehemiah before it draws a plan. With royal permission he returns, inspects the damage, and gathers people for the work. Families rebuild amid threats and fatigue. Restoration means more than stones: Nehemiah also confronts exploitation within the community.
entries.date: Persian-period restoration · fifth century BCE

entries.title: The people hear the book again
entries.summary: Ezra reads the law before a gathered people while others help them understand it. Tears give way to a call to share food and rejoice; the story of the people is heard again in their own rebuilt city. Scripture is not merely recovered as an object—it is read, explained, and lived together.
entries.date: Persian-period restoration · fifth century BCE

entries.title: A messenger before the Lord
entries.summary: Malachi challenges weary worship, injustice, and broken faithfulness. The book looks toward a messenger who prepares the way and toward Elijah’s coming. When the Gospels introduce John the Baptist, they deliberately bring these words back into view: the next chapter is connected to the old promises.
entries.date: Exile and Persian-period settings · some stories overlap era 07

entries.title: Between Persia and Rome
entries.summary: The opening of 1 Maccabees looks back to Alexander and the kingdoms divided among his successors. Greek-speaking political and cultural worlds form part of the background to later Jewish life. The road to the Gospels passes through living communities, contested loyalties, and changing empires—not an empty gap.
entries.date: Second Temple background · not four centuries of an empty story
entries.note: This is the Greek 1 Maccabees in the WEB ecumenical collection, not Ethiopian Meqabyan. It is identified here as a historical bridge; the two works must not be substituted for one another.

entries.title: The dedication Jesus remembers
entries.summary: After the temple’s desecration, Judas Maccabeus and his companions cleanse the sanctuary, rebuild the altar, and celebrate its dedication. John later places Jesus in Jerusalem during the Feast of Dedication, in winter. A named Gospel setting opens a doorway into the history between the Testaments.
entries.date: Rededication conventionally c. 164 BCE · John’s scene is centuries later
entries.note: The first reference is Greek 1 Maccabees, not Ethiopian Meqabyan. The later Gospel scene is linked, not assigned the rededication’s date.

entries.title: An empire, a client king & a coming child
entries.summary: The Gospels name rulers as well as villages: Matthew places Jesus’ birth under Herod, Luke names Augustus, and Luke’s account of John’s ministry names Tiberius and Pontius Pilate. These are stories told in a world of empire, taxation, local rulers, and ordinary families—not a kingdom waiting on an empty stage.
entries.date: Second Temple background · not four centuries of an empty story
entries.note: Matthew’s Herod setting and Luke’s reference to Quirinius raise a well-known chronological difficulty. The atlas preserves both accounts and does not claim to have resolved it.

entries.title: Waiting for consolation
entries.summary: Isaiah speaks of light, a child, and a shoot from Jesse; Luke introduces Simeon and Anna as people waiting for consolation and redemption. The Gospels tell Jesus’ story within Israel’s hopes. Those hopes were not one uniform political program, and Jesus’ way of fulfilling them repeatedly surprises those around Him.
entries.date: Second Temple background · not four centuries of an empty story

entries.title: The Jewish world Jesus calls home
entries.summary: Jesus’ family keeps Passover, He teaches in synagogues, and His conversations engage the Scriptures of Israel. Pharisees, Sadducees, priests, teachers, and ordinary worshippers do not all hold the same views. The Gospels’ debates belong within this varied Jewish world; they are not a portrait of an entire people as Jesus’ enemies.
entries.date: Second Temple background · not four centuries of an empty story

entries.title: Jesus · the Word made flesh
entries.summary: The promises converge on a person. Matthew introduces Jesus as Messiah, son of David and son of Abraham. Luke brings us to a child laid in a manger. John reaches back to “the beginning” and announces that the Word became flesh and dwelt among us. The center of this journey is Jesus: His life, His self-giving death, His resurrection, and His invitation to follow.
entries.date: Jesus’ life, death, resurrection & continuing reign
entries.note: The Gospel genealogies and infancy accounts are presented in their own voices. Joseph’s place in Matthew’s genealogy is not a claim that he is Jesus’ biological father.

echoes.label: The promise to Abraham and David
echoes.explanation: Matthew’s opening identifies Jesus through both names. Follow the earlier promises, then read how Matthew frames their continuation.

entries.title: In the beginning was the Word
entries.summary: John starts before Bethlehem. The Word is with God, the Word is God, and all things come into being through Him. Light shines in darkness; the Word becomes flesh and dwells among us. Read beside Genesis and the tabernacle story, this is an announcement about creation and God’s presence, not merely a new name on a family tree.
entries.date: John’s theological opening · the Word before creation and made flesh

echoes.label: Creation and dwelling
echoes.explanation: “In the beginning” recalls Genesis. God dwelling among His people also invites comparison with the tabernacle’s glory.

entries.title: Let it be to me according to your word
entries.summary: Gabriel comes to Mary in Nazareth with news of a son, a throne, and a kingdom without end. Mary asks how this can be; the answer points to the Holy Spirit and the power of the Most High. The promise to David is now spoken into the life of a young woman far from a royal palace.
entries.date: Birth often placed c. 6–4 BCE · exact chronology debated

echoes.label: A throne and a kingdom without end
echoes.explanation: Gabriel’s words about David’s throne connect Mary’s child with the promise spoken to David.

entries.title: Joseph receives a difficult promise
entries.summary: Joseph’s intention to separate quietly from Mary changes after a dream. He is told not to fear taking her as his wife and to name the child Jesus, because He will save His people from their sins. Matthew links the birth with Immanuel—God with us—and shows Joseph responding with action.
entries.date: Birth often placed c. 6–4 BCE · exact chronology debated
entries.note: Matthew explicitly applies Isaiah’s Immanuel passage to Jesus. Isaiah 7 also has its own original setting in the crisis facing King Ahaz; the connection does not erase that setting.

entries.title: Two mothers, one song of reversal
entries.summary: Mary visits Elizabeth, and the meeting becomes blessing and song. Mary praises the God who lifts the lowly, fills the hungry, and remembers His promise to Abraham. Her song belongs beside Hannah’s: the arrival of Jesus is announced as mercy that overturns ordinary measurements of greatness.
entries.date: Birth often placed c. 6–4 BCE · exact chronology debated

echoes.label: Hannah and Mary sing
echoes.explanation: Compare the raising of the lowly and the reversal of ordinary power in these two songs. The parallel does not make their settings identical.

entries.title: A name, a voice & a prepared road
entries.summary: Elizabeth’s child is named John, and Zechariah’s silence breaks into praise. His song looks toward salvation in David’s house and a child who will prepare the Lord’s ways. John’s story matters because it points beyond itself: the dawn he announces is about to arrive.
entries.date: Birth often placed c. 6–4 BCE · exact chronology debated

entries.title: Good news in a manger
entries.summary: Jesus is born in Bethlehem, David’s city, and laid in a manger. Luke places the announcement among ordinary travelers and shepherds, not among the empire’s celebrated victories. The child is proclaimed Savior, Christ, and Lord. The story’s center arrives with vulnerability before it is recognized in glory.
entries.date: Often placed c. 6–4 BCE · exact birth date is unknown

entries.title: The first invitation is to shepherds
entries.summary: In the fields outside Bethlehem, fear gives way to good news of great joy. The sign is a baby wrapped and lying in a manger. The shepherds go, see, tell, and return praising God; Mary keeps these things and ponders them. Wonder moves from the sky into a visit, then into a story shared.
entries.date: Birth often placed c. 6–4 BCE · exact chronology debated

entries.title: Simeon and Anna recognize the child
entries.summary: In Jerusalem’s temple, Simeon takes Jesus in his arms and speaks of light for the nations and glory for Israel. Anna gives thanks and speaks about the child to those waiting for redemption. Celebration carries a shadow too: Simeon tells Mary of opposition and a sword that will pierce her own soul.
entries.date: Birth often placed c. 6–4 BCE · exact chronology debated

entries.title: A star, a search & another road home
entries.summary: Visitors from the east come looking for the king of the Jews. In Jerusalem their question troubles Herod; in Bethlehem they offer gifts and worship the child. A dream sends them home another way. Matthew contrasts a ruler guarding his power with travelers ready to kneel before someone greater.
entries.date: Birth often placed c. 6–4 BCE · exact chronology debated
entries.note: Matthew does not state the visitors’ number or call them kings. Their arrival is not forced onto the same night as Luke’s shepherds.

entries.title: The child becomes a refugee
entries.summary: Warned in a dream, Joseph takes the child and His mother to Egypt while Herod orders violence in Bethlehem. After Herod’s death the family returns and settles in Nazareth. Matthew hears echoes of Israel’s earlier story: a threatened child, grief, Egypt, and a son called out of it.
entries.date: Birth often placed c. 6–4 BCE · exact chronology debated
entries.note: The Egypt marker is regional; Matthew does not supply an itinerary. Hosea’s original passage recalls Israel’s Exodus, which Matthew reuses in telling Jesus’ story.

entries.title: In My Father’s house
entries.summary: At twelve, Jesus stays behind in Jerusalem after Passover. Mary and Joseph find Him among the teachers, listening and asking questions. His answer about His Father’s house opens a question they do not yet fully understand. Luke then returns Him to Nazareth, growing in wisdom and stature.
entries.date: Jesus at twelve · Luke 2 does not specify a calendar year

entries.title: A voice in the wilderness
entries.summary: John calls people to repentance and baptizes in the Jordan region. The Gospels introduce him through Isaiah’s prepared road and Malachi’s messenger, while his clothing recalls Elijah. Yet John insists that the one coming after him is greater: his ministry is a doorway into Jesus’ story, not its destination.
entries.date: John’s public ministry · Luke names Tiberius’s fifteenth year
entries.note: The river pin indicates a region, not a securely located baptism site.

entries.title: The beloved Son at the Jordan
entries.summary: Jesus comes to John for baptism. The heavens open, the Spirit descends, and a voice names Him the beloved Son. Before the crowds, miracles, and confrontations, the Gospels place this declaration at the threshold of His public ministry. John’s witness points to Jesus as the Lamb of God.
entries.date: Public ministry · commonly placed in the late 20s / early 30s CE

entries.title: Forty days in the wilderness
entries.summary: In hunger and temptation, Jesus refuses to turn sonship into self-serving power. His answers draw from Deuteronomy: bread is not enough, God is not to be tested, and worship belongs to God alone. Israel’s wilderness story sounds again, now around the faithful Son preparing to announce the kingdom.
entries.date: Public ministry · commonly placed in the late 20s / early 30s CE
entries.note: Matthew and Luke arrange the temptations differently. This entry connects their shared themes without forcing an identical sequence.

echoes.label: The wilderness answers
echoes.explanation: Jesus’ replies draw from Deuteronomy’s account of Israel learning faithfulness in the wilderness.

entries.title: Bread in the wilderness, bread for the world
entries.summary: When the crowd recalls manna, Jesus takes the conversation beyond a remembered meal. Moses did not give the final bread from heaven; the Father gives the true bread, and Jesus identifies Himself as the bread of life. This is a Gospel connection back to Exodus, not a new date assigned to the wilderness story.
entries.date: Public ministry · commonly placed in the late 20s / early 30s CE
entries.note: This bridge entry is placed with John 6. The Exodus event itself belongs to the earlier wilderness period.

entries.title: Leave the nets. Come and see.
entries.summary: Jesus calls people into companionship before they understand where it will lead. Fishermen leave nets; Andrew brings Simon; Philip invites Nathanael to come and see. The Gospel accounts give distinct windows into these beginnings. The disciples will learn by walking, listening, failing, and being called again.
entries.date: Public ministry · commonly placed in the late 20s / early 30s CE

entries.title: The first sign at a wedding
entries.summary: At a wedding in Cana, the wine runs out. Mary brings the need to Jesus and tells the servants to do whatever He says. Water becomes wine, and John calls this the beginning of Jesus’ signs, revealing His glory. A household celebration becomes the setting for the disciples’ growing faith.
entries.date: Public ministry · commonly placed in the late 20s / early 30s CE

entries.title: Today this Scripture is fulfilled
entries.summary: In Nazareth’s synagogue, Jesus reads Isaiah’s announcement of good news to the poor, release, sight, and freedom. Then He says the Scripture is fulfilled in their hearing. Admiration turns toward anger when He recalls God’s mercy reaching a widow in Sidon and Naaman the Syrian. The kingdom will not be confined to hometown expectations.
entries.date: Public ministry · commonly placed in the late 20s / early 30s CE

echoes.label: Good news to the poor
echoes.explanation: Luke names Isaiah’s scroll. Read the original promise and Jesus’ announcement of its fulfillment together.

entries.title: A conversation after dark
entries.summary: Nicodemus comes to Jesus at night and hears about birth from above, the Spirit, and God’s love for the world. Jesus reaches back to Moses lifting the serpent in the wilderness to speak of the Son of Man being lifted up. A quiet conversation opens onto the meaning of the cross.
entries.date: Public ministry · commonly placed in the late 20s / early 30s CE

echoes.label: The lifted serpent and the lifted Son
echoes.explanation: John places Jesus’ comparison with Numbers inside the conversation about life and God’s love.

entries.title: Living water at the well
entries.summary: Jesus asks a Samaritan woman for a drink and offers living water. Their conversation crosses inherited hostility and moves through thirst, truth, and worship. She leaves her water jar to invite others to meet Him. A person outside the expected circle becomes the voice that brings a town to listen.
entries.date: Public ministry · commonly placed in the late 20s / early 30s CE

entries.title: Blessed are the unlikely
