entries.summary: Jesus calls the poor in spirit, the mourners, the meek, the merciful, and the peacemakers blessed. In the Sermon on the Mount, the kingdom’s life reaches into anger, reconciliation, desire, truthfulness, and love for enemies. The law and prophets are not discarded; the listener is invited into a searching, lived righteousness.
entries.date: Public ministry · commonly placed in the late 20s / early 30s CE
entries.note: Matthew’s sermon on the mountain and Luke’s sermon on a level place are allowed their own settings and emphases. Galilee is a regional marker, not an identified hillside.

entries.title: Teach us to pray
entries.summary: Jesus teaches His followers to address the Father with reverence and trust: His name, His kingdom, His will, daily bread, forgiveness, and deliverance. Prayer is neither a performance nor a way to overwhelm God with words. The prayer’s “us” keeps ordinary need and reconciliation inside a shared life.
entries.date: Public ministry · commonly placed in the late 20s / early 30s CE

entries.title: A roof opens. A man rises.
entries.summary: Friends carry a paralyzed man to Jesus and lower him through a roof when the crowd blocks the door. Jesus first announces forgiveness, then tells him to rise and walk. The scene brings friendship, mercy, and the question of His authority into one crowded room.
entries.date: Public ministry · commonly placed in the late 20s / early 30s CE

entries.title: Is it lawful to do good?
entries.summary: In debates about grain and a healing on the Sabbath, Jesus places human need and mercy at the center of the encounter. A man’s hand is restored while opponents watch. These disputes reveal sharply different judgments about faithfulness; they are not permission to caricature Judaism as a religion without compassion.
entries.date: Public ministry · commonly placed in the late 20s / early 30s CE

entries.title: Only say the word
entries.summary: A centurion seeks help for a desperately ill servant. His understanding of authority becomes a picture of trust: Jesus need only speak. Jesus marvels at the faith He encounters. The kingdom’s invitation is already pressing beyond the boundaries that the disciples might have expected.
entries.date: Public ministry · commonly placed in the late 20s / early 30s CE
entries.note: Matthew presents the appeal directly; Luke describes intermediaries. Both accounts remain available without rewriting one into the other.

entries.title: Do not weep
entries.summary: At Nain, Jesus meets a funeral procession for a widow’s only son. Moved with compassion, He tells her not to weep and calls the young man to rise. Luke’s wording recalls Elijah giving a restored son back to his mother: an older story of mercy sounds again as the crowd praises God.
entries.date: Public ministry · commonly placed in the late 20s / early 30s CE

entries.title: A kingdom told in seeds
entries.summary: A sower scatters seed across different soils. A mustard seed grows beyond its small beginning. Through parables Jesus invites listeners to hear, reconsider, and respond: the kingdom is not measured only by what looks impressive at the start. The explanation of the soils turns the question toward the hearer’s own reception.
entries.date: Public ministry · commonly placed in the late 20s / early 30s CE

entries.title: Who then is this?
entries.summary: A storm fills the boat while Jesus sleeps. The disciples wake Him in fear; He speaks, and the wind and sea become calm. Their question shifts from whether they will survive to who is with them. Scripture’s language about God stilling the sea gives their astonishment a deeper background.
entries.date: Public ministry · commonly placed in the late 20s / early 30s CE

entries.title: Two daughters, one interrupted journey
entries.summary: Jesus goes with Jairus toward a dying child, but a woman suffering years of bleeding reaches for His garment. He stops to address her as daughter. News arrives that the child has died; Jesus continues, takes her hand, and tells her to rise. A delay becomes part of a story in which neither person is overlooked.
entries.date: Public ministry · commonly placed in the late 20s / early 30s CE

entries.title: Enough for the multitude
entries.summary: With a hungry crowd before Him, Jesus receives a few loaves and fish, gives thanks, and distributes food through His disciples. Everyone eats, and baskets remain. All four Gospels tell this feeding; John draws the reader onward into a difficult conversation about the bread of life.
entries.date: Public ministry · commonly placed in the late 20s / early 30s CE
entries.note: The regional lake marker does not identify a certain feeding site. This is the feeding of the five thousand, distinct from the four thousand in Matthew and Mark.

entries.title: It is I. Do not be afraid.
entries.summary: The disciples struggle across the water and see Jesus coming toward them. Fear meets His reassurance. Matthew also tells of Peter stepping out, sinking, and being caught. The story is not about a disciple mastering the sea; it turns attention toward the one who reaches him in his fear.
entries.date: Public ministry · commonly placed in the late 20s / early 30s CE

entries.title: Will you also go away?
entries.summary: After the feeding, Jesus refuses to remain only the supplier of another meal. He speaks of Himself as the bread of life, given for the life of the world. Some listeners turn away at the difficulty of His words. Peter’s answer holds the question open in trust: to whom would they go, when Jesus has the words of eternal life?
entries.date: Public ministry · commonly placed in the late 20s / early 30s CE

entries.title: Mercy beyond the expected boundary
entries.summary: A Gentile mother asks Jesus to free her daughter. The conversation is difficult, and her reply about crumbs under the table is persistent and bold. Jesus grants her request. Mark and Matthew preserve an encounter that refuses to let the reader overlook a mother’s faith across an inherited boundary.
entries.date: Public ministry · commonly placed in the late 20s / early 30s CE
entries.note: Mark calls her a Greek, Syrophoenician by birth; Matthew calls her Canaanite. The summaries retain that distinction rather than flattening the accounts.

entries.title: You are the Christ
entries.summary: Near Caesarea Philippi, Jesus asks who the disciples say He is. Peter names Him as the Christ. Yet recognition does not immediately become understanding: when Jesus speaks of suffering and death, Peter resists. Jesus connects discipleship with taking up a cross, not with securing the kind of victory Peter imagined.
entries.date: Public ministry · commonly placed in the late 20s / early 30s CE

entries.title: Listen to Him
entries.summary: On a mountain, Jesus is transfigured before Peter, James, and John. Moses and Elijah appear, and the voice from the cloud calls the disciples to listen to the beloved Son. Luke says the conversation concerns the departure Jesus will accomplish in Jerusalem. Glory points toward the coming cross rather than away from it.
entries.date: Public ministry · commonly placed in the late 20s / early 30s CE
entries.note: The Gospels do not name this mountain. The atlas does not place an invented pin for it.

echoes.label: Moses, Elijah, and the beloved Son
echoes.explanation: The figures are explicitly identified. Luke connects their conversation with Jesus’ coming departure at Jerusalem.

entries.title: Who became a neighbor?
entries.summary: Asked who counts as a neighbor, Jesus tells of a wounded traveler, people who pass by, and a Samaritan who stops. Mercy is costly, practical, and offered across hostility. Jesus turns the question from drawing the right boundary around “my neighbor” toward becoming a neighbor to the person in need.
entries.date: Public ministry · commonly placed in the late 20s / early 30s CE
entries.note: This is a parable, not a separately dated event. Its Jerusalem–Jericho setting is part of the story, not a reconstructed journey.

entries.title: At His feet, in the middle of hospitality
entries.summary: Martha welcomes Jesus while Mary sits listening at His feet. Distracted by much serving, Martha asks Him to intervene. Jesus answers her anxiety with an invitation to the one needed thing. The scene honors the act of hearing Him without turning hospitality or work into enemies of faith.
entries.date: Public ministry · commonly placed in the late 20s / early 30s CE
entries.note: Luke does not name the village in this scene. Its placement at Bethany is not asserted from Luke alone.

entries.title: The father runs
entries.summary: A younger son wastes his inheritance and returns rehearsing a speech. His father runs to welcome him before he can bargain for a servant’s place. Outside the celebration, an older brother has his own struggle with grace. Jesus leaves the invitation sounding toward both sons—and toward those listening.
entries.date: Public ministry · commonly placed in the late 20s / early 30s CE
entries.note: The lost sheep, coin, and sons are parables told in response to criticism of Jesus welcoming sinners, not episodes on a historical calendar.

entries.title: One thing I know: now I see
entries.summary: Jesus refuses the assumption that a man’s blindness can be explained by assigning blame to him or his parents. After Jesus gives him sight, the man faces repeated questioning and exclusion. Jesus finds him again. The chapter gradually asks who truly sees, and who is unwilling to recognize what stands before them.
entries.date: Public ministry · commonly placed in the late 20s / early 30s CE

entries.title: The shepherd lays down His life
entries.summary: Jesus describes a shepherd who knows His sheep, calls them by name, and does not abandon them to danger. He lays down His life willingly and speaks of other sheep and one flock. Read beside Psalm 23 and Ezekiel’s critique of failed shepherds, this image becomes a claim about the care and leadership God’s people need.
entries.date: Public ministry · commonly placed in the late 20s / early 30s CE

entries.title: I am the resurrection and the life
entries.summary: At Bethany, Martha meets Jesus with grief and trust while Mary weeps at His feet. Jesus Himself weeps. Before Lazarus is called from the tomb, Jesus identifies resurrection and life with Himself. The sign brings joy to a household and intensifies the decision of opponents to put Jesus to death.
entries.date: Public ministry · commonly placed in the late 20s / early 30s CE

entries.title: Let the children come
entries.summary: When the disciples try to turn children away, Jesus is indignant. He welcomes them, takes them in His arms, and speaks of receiving the kingdom like a child. The people a hurried group might treat as interruptions are placed at the center of His lesson about belonging.
entries.date: Public ministry · commonly placed in the late 20s / early 30s CE

entries.title: Today salvation has come to this house
entries.summary: Zacchaeus climbs a tree to see Jesus and discovers that Jesus has come looking for him. An invitation to his house unsettles the crowd. His response involves generosity and restitution, not merely a private feeling. Jesus describes His mission as seeking and saving the lost.
entries.date: Public ministry · commonly placed in the late 20s / early 30s CE

entries.title: Your king comes to you, humble
entries.summary: Jesus enters Jerusalem on a donkey as people spread garments and branches along the way. The Gospels connect the scene with Zechariah’s humble king and the language of Psalm 118. The city receives a royal sign, but the kind of kingship Jesus will reveal is about to overturn expectations.
entries.date: Passion and resurrection · commonly dated around 30 or 33 CE

entries.title: A house of prayer for all nations
entries.summary: Jesus confronts buying and selling in the temple and invokes Isaiah’s house of prayer and Jeremiah’s warning about a den of robbers. His action challenges what the sanctuary has become. The conflict sharpens as leaders question His authority and the crowds continue to listen.
entries.date: Passion and resurrection · commonly dated around 30 or 33 CE
entries.note: The Synoptic Gospels place this action in Jesus’ final Jerusalem ministry; John places a temple action near the beginning. Both passages are available without asserting that their chronology is identical.

entries.title: Love God. Love your neighbor.
entries.summary: In a series of questions about authority, resurrection, and faithfulness, Jesus names love of God and love of neighbor as the heart of the commandments. He joins Deuteronomy and Leviticus, not a newly invented ethic detached from Israel’s Scriptures. Mark’s account ends with a teacher whom Jesus calls not far from the kingdom.
entries.date: Passion and resurrection · commonly dated around 30 or 33 CE

entries.title: Watch, endure & do not be led astray
entries.summary: Looking toward the temple, Jesus speaks of its destruction, distress, deceptive claims, and the coming of the Son of Man. His followers are told to endure and stay awake, not to possess the day and hour. The discourse prepares readers for costly faithfulness and connects with Daniel’s language of crisis and vindication.
entries.date: Passion and resurrection · commonly dated around 30 or 33 CE
entries.note: Readers differ over how these sayings relate to Jerusalem’s destruction and the final coming of Christ. The atlas distinguishes the questions rather than turning the discourse into a modern prediction calendar.

entries.title: A costly gift before the burial
entries.summary: At Bethany, costly perfume is poured out on Jesus. Objections focus on waste; Jesus speaks of burial and a deed that will be remembered with the good news. John names Mary and places the scene with Martha and Lazarus. The gift recognizes something about the coming death that others struggle to face.
entries.date: Passion and resurrection · commonly dated around 30 or 33 CE
entries.note: John and the Synoptic accounts have distinct details and placement. Luke 7’s anointing is not silently merged into this Bethany scene.

entries.title: A table, a covenant & a coming kingdom
entries.summary: Jesus shares bread and a cup with His disciples and speaks of His body and blood given for them. Passover memory becomes the setting for a new-covenant promise. Betrayal is near, but the table is also pointed toward the kingdom. Paul later passes on this meal as a proclamation of the Lord’s death until He comes.
entries.date: Passion and resurrection · commonly dated around 30 or 33 CE
entries.note: The Gospels’ presentation of the meal and Passover chronology is not forced into a single uncontested calendar reconstruction.

entries.title: The Lord takes the servant’s place
entries.summary: Knowing where He has come from and where He is going, Jesus rises from supper, takes a towel, and washes His disciples’ feet. Peter struggles to receive it. Jesus turns the act into an example and gives a command to love one another as He has loved them. His greatness is expressed in service.
entries.date: Passion and resurrection · commonly dated around 30 or 33 CE

entries.title: Abide in Me
entries.summary: Jesus speaks of the vine and branches: life and fruitfulness come through remaining in Him. He calls His disciples friends, commands love, and promises the Spirit’s witness amid opposition. His prayer reaches beyond the room toward those who will believe through their word, asking that they may be one.
entries.date: Passion and resurrection · commonly dated around 30 or 33 CE

entries.title: Not My will, but Yours
entries.summary: In the garden, Jesus prays in deep distress while His companions struggle to stay awake. He does not disguise the cost before Him. His prayer entrusts His will to the Father, and betrayal arrives with an armed crowd. The one who could speak peace to a storm now enters suffering without abandoning His mission.
entries.date: Passion and resurrection · commonly dated around 30 or 33 CE

entries.title: Before the rooster crows
entries.summary: Peter has promised loyalty, but in the courtyard he repeatedly denies knowing Jesus. The rooster’s call brings Jesus’ warning back to him, and he weeps. This is not Peter’s final scene: the resurrection accounts will bring him from failure toward a renewed call to care for Jesus’ sheep.
entries.date: Passion and resurrection · commonly dated around 30 or 33 CE

entries.title: The Son of Man before His judges
entries.summary: Jesus faces questioning, conflicting testimony, mockery, and violence. In Mark, His answer about the Son of Man invokes Daniel and the language of sitting at God’s right hand. The scene places the promised king under judgment while the narrative invites readers to ask who truly holds authority.
entries.date: Passion and resurrection · commonly dated around 30 or 33 CE
entries.note: The accounts identify particular authorities and participants. They do not justify blaming Jewish people collectively for Jesus’ death; Jesus and His first followers are themselves Jewish.

entries.title: My kingdom is not from this world
entries.summary: Before the Roman governor, Jesus is questioned about kingship. John records His answer that His kingdom is not from this world and His mission bears witness to truth. A crowd, a prisoner named Barabbas, mock royal clothing, and political pressure surround the decision. Pilate hands Jesus over to be crucified.
entries.date: Passion and resurrection · commonly dated around 30 or 33 CE

entries.title: The King gives His life
entries.summary: Jesus is crucified outside Jerusalem under a royal charge. The Gospels let us hear abandonment, forgiveness, care for His mother, and trust in the Father through their distinct accounts. The curtain tears; a centurion responds. At the center of Christian faith stands this self-giving death—not a detour from Jesus’ mission, but its costly fulfillment.
entries.date: Crucifixion under Pontius Pilate · 30 and 33 CE are common proposals
entries.note: The entries keep the Gospel accounts distinct rather than presenting a reconstructed sequence of every saying. The hill’s precise location is not asserted by a separate map pin.

echoes.label: The psalm and the suffering servant
echoes.explanation: The Gospel cry draws directly on Psalm 22. Isaiah 53 provides language that New Testament writers use when speaking of Jesus’ suffering.

entries.title: A borrowed tomb, a watched ending
entries.summary: Joseph of Arimathea asks for Jesus’ body and places it in a tomb. John names Nicodemus as another participant; the Synoptic accounts remember women seeing where He is laid. The story pauses with grief and a real burial, not with the disciples already expecting how the next morning will unfold.
entries.date: Passion and resurrection · commonly dated around 30 or 33 CE

entries.title: He is not here. He has risen.
entries.summary: Women come to the tomb and find that death has not kept Jesus. The Gospel accounts describe the discovery and its witnesses in different ways, but the announcement changes the direction of the whole story. The crucified Jesus is risen. Fear, joy, doubt, and recognition now lead His followers into a new beginning.
entries.date: Passion and resurrection · commonly dated around 30 or 33 CE
entries.note: Witnesses, messengers, and the order of appearances differ across accounts. This entry does not manufacture one exhaustive itinerary. Mark 16:1–8 is used here without depending on the disputed longer ending.

entries.title: He calls her by name
entries.summary: Mary Magdalene stands weeping near the tomb. She sees Jesus but does not recognize Him until He says her name. Grief becomes recognition and then a commission: she goes to the disciples with the announcement that she has seen the Lord. The resurrection’s good news is entrusted to her voice.
entries.date: Passion and resurrection · commonly dated around 30 or 33 CE

entries.title: Their hearts burned on the road
entries.summary: Two disciples leave Jerusalem carrying disappointed hopes. A stranger walks with them and opens the Scriptures, beginning with Moses and the prophets. At the table, in the breaking of bread, they recognize Jesus. They hurry back: the older story has not been abandoned, but has become newly legible around the risen Christ.
entries.date: Passion and resurrection · commonly dated around 30 or 33 CE
entries.note: Several sites have been proposed for Emmaus. The atlas does not choose one as certain or draw an invented route.

echoes.label: The older story opened around Jesus
echoes.explanation: Luke describes Jesus interpreting Moses and the prophets but does not list every passage in the conversation. The atlas does not invent that list.

entries.title: My Lord and my God
entries.summary: Thomas is absent when Jesus first appears to the gathered disciples and resists their report. Jesus meets him with the wounds he demanded to see. Thomas answers with a confession, and Jesus speaks of those who will believe without having seen. John then explains why the signs in his Gospel were written.
entries.date: Passion and resurrection · commonly dated around 30 or 33 CE

entries.title: Do you love Me? Feed My sheep.
entries.summary: Beside the lake, the risen Jesus prepares a meal after the disciples’ night of fishing. He asks Peter about love and entrusts him with caring for His sheep. Peter’s denial is not the last word over his life. The call “Follow Me” returns, now with an understanding that love will carry a cost.
entries.date: Passion and resurrection · commonly dated around 30 or 33 CE

entries.title: I am with you always
entries.summary: The risen Jesus meets His disciples in Galilee, where worship and doubt are both named. He sends them to make disciples of all nations, baptizing and teaching, and promises His presence to the end of the age. Matthew’s story that began with “God with us” ends with Jesus’ assurance that He remains with His people.
entries.date: Passion and resurrection · commonly dated around 30 or 33 CE

entries.title: Witnesses, not owners of the timetable
entries.summary: Before Jesus is taken up, the disciples ask about the kingdom’s restoration. He redirects them from times reserved to the Father toward the Spirit’s power and their calling as witnesses: Jerusalem, Judea, Samaria, and the ends of the earth. His departure is not the end of His story; Acts follows what happens next.
entries.date: Passion and resurrection · commonly dated around 30 or 33 CE

entries.title: The Spirit comes. The story goes outward.
entries.summary: At Pentecost, the gathered followers of Jesus hear wind and see tongues like fire. People from many places hear God’s mighty works in their own languages. Peter connects the moment to Joel’s promise and proclaims the crucified and risen Jesus. A community begins to grow around repentance, baptism, teaching, meals, and prayer.
entries.date: First-century settings · letters are grouped by theme, not asserted writing date

echoes.label: Many languages, one announcement
echoes.explanation: Babel and Pentecost both foreground language and scattered peoples. Acts explicitly quotes Joel; a “reversal of Babel” is a common theological comparison, not a phrase Acts itself uses.

entries.title: Breaking bread, sharing life
entries.summary: Acts describes believers devoting themselves to the apostles’ teaching, fellowship, the breaking of bread, and prayers. Possessions become resources for meeting need. The picture is neither an account of instant perfection nor a private spirituality: the risen Jesus is confessed through a shared, practical life.
entries.date: First-century settings · letters are grouped by theme, not asserted writing date

entries.title: A witness sees the Son of Man
entries.summary: Chosen in the community’s response to overlooked widows, Stephen becomes a public witness. His speech retells Israel’s story, and his vision names the Son of Man at God’s right hand. As he is killed, he prays for his attackers. Saul stands nearby, a figure whose own story is about to turn.
entries.date: First-century settings · letters are grouped by theme, not asserted writing date
entries.note: Stephen’s speech is a dispute narrated within the first-century biblical story, not grounds for hostility toward Jewish communities.

entries.title: Good news crosses into Samaria
entries.summary: Persecution scatters believers, and Philip announces the Messiah in Samaria. The story that Jesus outlined before His ascension begins to unfold beyond Jerusalem. Joy, healing, baptism, and an encounter with Simon also raise a sharp question: God’s gift cannot be purchased as spiritual power.
entries.date: First-century settings · letters are grouped by theme, not asserted writing date

entries.title: From Isaiah’s scroll to Jesus
entries.summary: On the road toward Gaza, Philip meets an Ethiopian court official reading Isaiah. “Who is the prophet talking about?” becomes the opening for Philip to proclaim Jesus. The official asks for baptism and goes on his way rejoicing. A reader from the African world is not on the edge of this story—he is one of its memorable witnesses to the widening good news.
entries.date: First-century settings · letters are grouped by theme, not asserted writing date
entries.note: Acts identifies the official with the Kandake’s court; this ancient “Ethiopia” is commonly connected with Kush, south of Egypt, not simply mapped onto the borders of modern Ethiopia. Later church traditions are distinct from what Acts explicitly narrates. Verse 37 appears as a labeled textual note in this reading edition.

entries.title: Saul, Saul, why do you persecute Me?
entries.summary: Traveling to Damascus to arrest followers of the Way, Saul is confronted by the risen Jesus. Blind and dependent, he receives help from Ananias, who must face his own fear in approaching him. The persecutor becomes a witness. Acts retells the encounter later as Paul explains the calling that redirected his life.
entries.date: First-century settings · letters are grouped by theme, not asserted writing date

entries.title: God shows no partiality
entries.summary: Cornelius receives a message to send for Peter; Peter receives a vision that challenges his boundaries. In the encounter that follows, Peter announces Jesus’ life, death, and resurrection. The Spirit comes upon Gentile hearers, and baptism follows. The church must recognize what God has already done.
entries.date: First-century settings · letters are grouped by theme, not asserted writing date

entries.title: A church learns to send
entries.summary: In Antioch, the message reaches a widening circle. Barnabas sees grace at work and brings Saul to help teach. Acts says the disciples are first called Christians here. Later, while the community worships and fasts, Barnabas and Saul are set apart and sent; a local church becomes a doorway to wider journeys.
entries.date: First-century settings · letters are grouped by theme, not asserted writing date

entries.title: Across Cyprus and into new towns
entries.summary: Sent from Antioch, Barnabas and Saul travel through Cyprus and into communities of southern Asia Minor. They speak in synagogues, meet interest and resistance, and turn toward Gentile hearers. In Lystra, a healing is misunderstood as a visit from gods. On the return, they strengthen disciples and appoint elders.
entries.date: First-century settings · letters are grouped by theme, not asserted writing date
entries.note: The map links named stops for orientation, not reconstructed sea lanes or roads. Acts 13–14 supplies the itinerary; the conventional numbered “missionary journeys” are editorial labels.

entries.title: A table wide enough for the nations
entries.summary: As Gentiles join the movement, a dispute arises over circumcision and the law of Moses. Peter recalls God’s action among Gentiles; Barnabas and Paul report their work; James turns to the prophets. The decision in Acts 15 seeks a way for this growing community to live together without denying what grace has done.
entries.date: First-century settings · letters are grouped by theme, not asserted writing date
entries.note: Acts and Paul’s letters offer distinct perspectives on early disputes. This entry does not assume that every related episode can be dated or aligned without debate.

entries.title: The Lord opens Lydia’s heart
entries.summary: A vision redirects Paul toward Macedonia. At a place of prayer outside Philippi, Lydia listens, receives the message, and opens her home. Acts introduces the new work through a woman’s response and hospitality before it describes the city’s prison. The movement grows around households as well as public speeches.
entries.date: First-century settings · letters are grouped by theme, not asserted writing date

entries.title: Songs in the prison
entries.summary: Paul and Silas are beaten and imprisoned after a confrontation over an enslaved girl’s exploitation. At midnight they pray and sing. An earthquake opens the doors, but they stay; the jailer’s crisis becomes a question about salvation, then a shared meal and care for their wounds.
entries.date: First-century settings · letters are grouped by theme, not asserted writing date

entries.title: The unknown God and the risen one
entries.summary: In Athens, Paul reasons in the synagogue and marketplace, then addresses hearers at the Areopagus. He begins with their religious world and speaks of the Creator, repentance, judgment, and the man God raised from the dead. Some mock, some want to hear more, and some believe. Resurrection remains the point of decision.
entries.date: First-century settings · letters are grouped by theme, not asserted writing date

entries.title: Tentmakers, teachers & a growing church
entries.summary: At Corinth, Paul works with Aquila and Priscilla while teaching about Jesus. Later, this couple helps Apollos understand the way more accurately. Their household connects travel, craft, hospitality, and teaching. Paul’s letters will address the difficult work of becoming one body amid rivalry and difference.
entries.date: First-century settings · letters are grouped by theme, not asserted writing date

entries.title: The word grows in a city of competing loyalties
entries.summary: Paul’s extended work in Ephesus brings teaching, changed loyalties, and public conflict. Some abandon magical practices; artisans fear the effect of the movement on the trade around Artemis. Acts shows the good news entering a city’s religious and economic life, not merely winning a private argument.
entries.date: First-century settings · letters are grouped by theme, not asserted writing date

entries.title: A witness in custody
entries.summary: Paul’s return to Jerusalem leads to arrest, disputed accusations, and hearings before Roman officials. He speaks of his hope in resurrection and recounts his encounter with Jesus. His appeal to Caesar will carry the witness toward Rome, but as a prisoner rather than a triumphant imperial visitor.
entries.date: First-century settings · letters are grouped by theme, not asserted writing date

entries.title: Hope through the storm
entries.summary: A journey to Rome becomes a long struggle against wind and sea. Paul encourages those aboard, food is shared, and the ship is lost while the people reach land. On Malta, strangers show extraordinary kindness. The mission continues through vulnerability and hospitality rather than control of the journey.
entries.date: First-century settings · letters are grouped by theme, not asserted writing date
entries.note: Acts names ports and episodes, but exact sailing tracks are reconstructed differently. The map’s connecting line is not a claim to trace the storm.

entries.title: The story ends with an open door
entries.summary: Paul reaches Rome in custody, yet receives visitors and teaches about the Lord Jesus Christ with boldness. Acts ends with the message unhindered, not with a completed biography of every apostle. The story that began in Jerusalem has reached the imperial capital—and its final scene still faces outward.
entries.date: First-century settings · letters are grouped by theme, not asserted writing date
entries.note: Later traditions about Paul’s death are not presented as events narrated in Acts.

entries.title: One body. A more excellent way.
entries.summary: The letters guide communities learning to follow Jesus together. Paul describes many gifts within one body, then names love as indispensable. Romans calls believers to overcome evil with good; Galatians speaks of the Spirit’s fruit; John insists that love of God and love of others cannot be separated.
entries.date: First-century settings · letters are grouped by theme, not asserted writing date

entries.title: A living faith has hands
entries.summary: Ephesians speaks of salvation by grace through faith and of being created for good works. James confronts a claim to faith that leaves a hungry neighbor unfed. Read in their own arguments, these passages turn the reader away from boasting and toward a life in which trust becomes visible as mercy.
entries.date: First-century settings · letters are grouped by theme, not asserted writing date
entries.note: Christian traditions explain the relation of faith, justification, and works differently. The atlas invites comparison of the passages rather than declaring those debates closed.

entries.title: Joy shaped like self-giving
entries.summary: Philippians calls a divided or anxious community toward the mind of Christ: humility, service, and hope. Its portrait of Jesus’ self-emptying and exaltation anchors an invitation to rejoice. Second Corinthians likewise connects treasure with fragile vessels and reconciliation with Christ, not with an appearance of invulnerability.
entries.date: First-century settings · letters are grouped by theme, not asserted writing date

entries.title: Receive him as a beloved brother
entries.summary: Paul appeals to Philemon concerning Onesimus, asking that he be received no longer merely as a slave but as a beloved brother. The short letter makes reconciliation concrete and personal, while leaving questions that later readers continue to wrestle with. Christian belonging presses against an existing social hierarchy.
entries.date: First-century settings · letters are grouped by theme, not asserted writing date
entries.note: The letter does not explicitly tell us every circumstance of Onesimus’s separation from Philemon or the eventual outcome. Those details are not filled in as facts.

entries.title: Guard the good entrusted to you
entries.summary: Letters to Timothy and Titus speak of teaching, character, care, and leadership. Second and Third John show smaller communities wrestling with truth and hospitality; First Peter calls believers to bear witness through their conduct. These voices help the atlas follow Jesus beyond the journeys into the daily life of His people.
entries.date: First-century settings · letters are grouped by theme, not asserted writing date
entries.note: The authorship and dates of several New Testament letters are debated. This thematic stop is not an assertion that all were written at the same moment.

entries.title: A priest who understands weakness
entries.summary: Hebrews invites readers to approach God with confidence because Jesus is a high priest who knows human weakness. Its argument reaches back to Melchizedek, priesthood, covenant, and sanctuary. These older threads are not discarded: the letter rereads them around Jesus’ once-for-all self-offering and continuing intercession.
entries.date: First-century settings · letters are grouped by theme, not asserted writing date

entries.title: Jude remembers Enoch
entries.summary: Jude explicitly names Enoch, the seventh from Adam, and cites his announcement of the Lord coming with holy ones for judgment. Read the words beside 1 Enoch 1: the Ethiopian-preserved text is part of the conversation within the New Testament itself. Jude’s warning ends in an invitation to mercy and a doxology of hope.
entries.date: First-century settings · letters are grouped by theme, not asserted writing date
entries.note: This is an explicit textual connection. Jude’s use of Enoch does not by itself settle the canonical status of every part of 1 Enoch for all Christian traditions.

echoes.label: Enoch named inside the New Testament
echoes.explanation: Jude names Enoch and cites the coming of the Lord with holy ones. Open the passages side by side in thought, preserving each edition’s wording.

entries.title: Because Christ has been raised
entries.summary: Paul makes the resurrection of Jesus the foundation of hope for those who belong to Him. First Corinthians 15 speaks of Christ as firstfruits and of death’s defeat; First Thessalonians offers comfort for those grieving. Hope is not a reason to abandon ordinary faithfulness, but a reason that labor in the Lord is not in vain.
entries.date: First-century settings · letters are grouped by theme, not asserted writing date

entries.title: Hope without a counterfeit countdown
entries.summary: Second Thessalonians warns against being quickly shaken by claims about the day of the Lord. Second Peter joins hope for new heavens and a new earth with a call to holy and patient living. The letters give urgency and endurance without handing readers a reliable date calculator.
entries.date: First-century settings · letters are grouped by theme, not asserted writing date
entries.note: Interpretations of these passages vary. Their place in the atlas is thematic, not a claim that their images produce a settled modern timeline.

entries.title: The revelation of Jesus Christ
entries.summary: John, on Patmos, hears a voice and turns to see one like a son of man among seven lampstands. The figure identifies Himself as the living one who was dead and is alive forever. Revelation opens with Jesus, not a code to be solved apart from Him: the churches are addressed by the risen Lord who knows them.
entries.date: Vision sequence, not a dated schedule of future events
entries.note: The author calls himself John. Whether he is the same John associated with the Fourth Gospel is disputed; the atlas does not silently treat that identification as settled.

echoes.label: The lampstands are explained
echoes.explanation: Revelation 1:20 identifies the lampstands as churches and the stars as their angels. Start with what the book itself explains before adding a proposed decoding.

entries.title: Seven churches, seven searching messages
entries.summary: The risen Jesus addresses communities in seven cities of Roman Asia. He knows their work, suffering, compromise, love, and need for repentance. Each message asks hearers to listen to what the Spirit says. The book’s extraordinary visions begin with the practical question of how real communities remain faithful.
entries.date: Vision sequence, not a dated schedule of future events

entries.title: Ephesus · return to your first love
entries.summary: The church’s work and endurance are recognized, but its abandoned first love cannot be excused by its other strengths. Jesus calls it to remember, repent, and do its first works. The promise to the conqueror reaches all the way back to the tree of life.
entries.date: Vision sequence, not a dated schedule of future events

entries.title: Smyrna · faithful through suffering
entries.summary: The one who died and lives again addresses a poor and afflicted community as rich. The message does not promise that suffering will disappear; it calls for faithfulness and promises the crown of life. The second death will not have the final word.
entries.date: Vision sequence, not a dated schedule of future events

entries.title: Pergamum · witness amid compromise
entries.summary: The community is praised for holding fast even when Antipas was killed, but challenged over teaching compared with Balaam’s stumbling block. Jesus promises hidden manna and a white stone with a new name. The precise social symbolism of the stone is debated; the invitation is to hear and remain faithful.
entries.date: Vision sequence, not a dated schedule of future events

entries.title: Thyatira · love, endurance & discernment
entries.summary: Love, service, faith, and growing works are recognized, while a teacher called Jezebel is condemned for leading others astray. The name recalls an earlier biblical story rather than proving this is the ancient queen herself. The message joins discernment with a call to hold fast.
entries.date: Vision sequence, not a dated schedule of future events

entries.title: Sardis · wake up
entries.summary: A reputation for life conceals a community described as dead. The call is to wake up, strengthen what remains, remember what was received, and keep it. White garments and the book of life frame the promise: public reputation is not the measure of faithfulness.
entries.date: Vision sequence, not a dated schedule of future events

entries.title: Philadelphia · an open door
entries.summary: The one holding the key of David speaks to a community with little power that has kept His word. An open door and a new name become images of belonging. The promise looks toward the city of God, the new Jerusalem coming down from heaven.
entries.date: Vision sequence, not a dated schedule of future events

entries.title: Laodicea · the door and the shared meal
entries.summary: A community confident in its wealth is confronted with its actual need. The vivid charge of lukewarmness leads to an invitation to repentance and fellowship. Jesus stands at the door and knocks; the promised meal is addressed here to a church being called back into communion.
entries.date: Vision sequence, not a dated schedule of future events

entries.title: A door opens into the throne room
entries.summary: John sees a throne, a rainbow, elders, lamps, and living creatures whose worship never ceases. Echoes of Isaiah and Ezekiel place the scene within Scripture’s older visions of divine holiness. Before the book shows the powers that frighten the earth, it shows the reader the throne that is not empty.
entries.date: Vision sequence, not a dated schedule of future events

echoes.label: Holy, holy, holy—and living creatures
echoes.explanation: Isaiah’s worship and Ezekiel’s living creatures are close scriptural neighbors of Revelation’s throne scene.

entries.title: The Lion is a Lamb who was slain
entries.summary: John hears of the Lion of Judah and the Root of David, but when he looks he sees a Lamb standing as though slain. The Lamb is worthy to open the scroll because He has redeemed people from every tribe, language, people, and nation. Revelation’s center of victory carries the marks of Jesus’ self-giving death.
entries.date: Vision sequence, not a dated schedule of future events
entries.note: The contrast between what John hears and what he sees is part of the text itself. The Lamb is not a separate rival to the Lion.

echoes.label: Hear a Lion. See a Lamb.
echoes.explanation: John hears the royal names, then sees the slain-yet-standing Lamb. Compare Judah’s lion and Jesse’s root without losing the startling turn in Revelation 5.

entries.title: The seals and the four horsemen
entries.summary: As the Lamb opens the seals, horses and riders bring images of conquest, war, scarcity, and death. The vision then hears the cry of the slain and shows a cosmic upheaval before the day of wrath. Zechariah’s horses provide an earlier visual vocabulary, though Revelation gives the imagery its own role.
entries.date: Vision sequence, not a dated schedule of future events
entries.note: Interpretations of the first rider and the sequence differ. No rider is assigned to a named modern country or event as a settled identification.

echoes.label: Horses before the horsemen
echoes.explanation: Zechariah sees colored horses and chariots sent through the earth. Revelation reworks horse imagery in the opening of the seals; each vision still has its own meaning.

entries.title: A numbered people, an unnumbered multitude
entries.summary: John hears the number of the sealed from Israel’s tribes, then sees a multitude no one can count from every nation. They stand before the throne and the Lamb, who shepherds them to springs of living water. Numbers, tribal names, and worldwide worship invite close reading rather than a quick census calculation.
entries.date: Vision sequence, not a dated schedule of future events
entries.note: Readers differ on how the 144,000 and the great multitude relate and whether the number is literal or symbolic. The text’s twelve-by-twelve-by-a-thousand pattern can be noticed without settling that debate.

echoes.label: A seal before judgment
echoes.explanation: Compare Ezekiel’s marking of mourners with the sealing in Revelation. The Lamb’s care for the multitude is as central as the number John hears.

entries.title: Trumpets, plagues & a wounded creation
entries.summary: Trumpet blasts bring images of fire, blood, darkened lights, locusts, and disaster. The Exodus plagues are part of the imagery’s scriptural background, while the fractions and repeated sequences give Revelation its own pattern. The visions confront idolatry and hardened refusal to turn, not just curiosity about catastrophes.
entries.date: Vision sequence, not a dated schedule of future events
entries.note: The relationship among seals, trumpets, and bowls is debated: some read a sequence, others see overlapping or recapitulated perspectives. The atlas follows the book’s reading order only.

echoes.label: An Exodus vocabulary
echoes.explanation: Water becoming blood, darkness, and locusts recall Egypt’s plagues. Similar imagery does not by itself fix a modern date for the vision.

entries.title: Sweet in the mouth, bitter in the stomach
entries.summary: A mighty angel holds a little open scroll. John is told to eat it; its sweetness becomes bitterness within him, and he must prophesy again. Ezekiel’s earlier call also involved eating a scroll. Receiving a prophetic word means taking it into one’s life, including its difficult burden.
entries.date: Vision sequence, not a dated schedule of future events

echoes.label: The prophet eats a scroll
echoes.explanation: Both Ezekiel and John receive the word through an enacted image of eating. Notice the sweetness and the differing emphasis on bitterness.

entries.title: Two witnesses, two olive trees
entries.summary: Revelation describes two witnesses as olive trees and lampstands before the Lord. Their testimony, suffering, apparent defeat, and vindication use imagery recalling Zechariah, Moses, and Elijah. Their story asks what faithful witness looks like when violent power appears to have the last word.
entries.date: Vision sequence, not a dated schedule of future events
entries.note: Some readers identify two individual future witnesses; others understand a corporate or symbolic testimony. The text’s named images are distinguished from those competing identifications.

echoes.label: Olive trees and lampstands
echoes.explanation: Revelation calls its witnesses olive trees and lampstands. Zechariah supplies an earlier scene of lamps, oil, and two anointed ones.

entries.title: The woman, the child & the dragon
entries.summary: A woman clothed with the sun, with the moon under her feet and twelve stars on her head, gives birth while a dragon waits to devour. The child is caught up to God and His throne. Revelation identifies the dragon as the ancient serpent, the devil and Satan; the accuser is overcome through the Lamb’s blood and faithful testimony.
entries.date: Vision sequence, not a dated schedule of future events
entries.note: The woman is read in relation to Israel, Mary, and the church in different traditions, sometimes in layered ways. Those readings are not flattened into a single uncontested identification.

echoes.label: Sun, moon, stars—and an ancient serpent
echoes.explanation: Joseph’s dream has sun, moon, and stars. Genesis has the serpent. Revelation itself identifies its dragon as the ancient serpent, devil, and Satan; the woman’s interpretation remains debated.

entries.title: When power demands worship
entries.summary: A beast rises from the sea with features recalling Daniel’s beasts. Another beast promotes its authority and directs worship toward it. The vision binds coercive power, deception, violence, and worship together. Its challenge is not merely to recognize a monster, but to discern what asks for the allegiance owed to God.
entries.date: Vision sequence, not a dated schedule of future events
entries.note: Roman imperial power is a major historical context in scholarship; Christian readings also differ over continuing and future fulfillment. No modern person or technology is identified as the beast by this atlas.

echoes.label: Daniel’s beasts return in a composite
echoes.explanation: Compare the leopard, bear, lion, horns, and blasphemous power. Daniel and Revelation do not use every detail in exactly the same way.

entries.title: The mark, the name & 666
entries.summary: Revelation connects the beast’s mark with its name or number and with the pressure to participate in buying and selling. The reader is invited to calculate a number: 666 in this edition. Compare the scene with the Lamb’s followers bearing His name in the next chapter—the contest concerns worship, identity, and allegiance.
entries.date: Vision sequence, not a dated schedule of future events
entries.note: Ancient name-number calculation is a serious avenue of interpretation; Nero Caesar is one prominent historical proposal, not a settled identification imposed here. Some manuscripts read 616. The reading room displays its named edition, 666; current people, payment systems, and devices are not labeled as fulfillments.

echoes.label: Two kinds of belonging
echoes.explanation: The beast’s mark and number are followed by the Lamb’s people bearing His name and His Father’s name. Read the chapter boundary as a connection, not an interruption.

entries.title: A name, a song & an enduring people
entries.summary: Against the beasts’ claims stands the Lamb on Mount Zion, with a people bearing His and His Father’s names. A new song, angelic announcements, and harvest imagery follow. The chapter calls for the endurance of the saints and contrasts faithfulness to the Lamb with worship of the beast.
entries.date: Vision sequence, not a dated schedule of future events
entries.note: Zion appears within the vision; it is not turned into a mapped military assembly or an assigned future date.

entries.title: The song of Moses and the Lamb
entries.summary: Those who overcome sing the song of Moses and the Lamb before the bowls are poured out. Plague imagery returns: sores, blood, darkness, and upheaval. The Exodus memory is explicit in the song, but Revelation places deliverance and judgment around the Lamb and the nations’ worship.
entries.date: Vision sequence, not a dated schedule of future events

echoes.label: Moses and the Lamb, together
echoes.explanation: Revelation names the song of Moses and the Lamb. Exodus’s deliverance song provides a revealing comparison before the bowls.

entries.title: Armageddon: a name inside a vision
entries.summary: Within the sixth bowl, deceptive spirits gather kings for battle, and the place is named in Hebrew as Armageddon. An interruption calls the reader to stay awake. The vision moves on to the seventh bowl and the downfall of Babylon; its purpose is not to provide a modern battlefield itinerary.
entries.date: Vision sequence, not a dated schedule of future events
entries.note: The name is often associated with Har-Megiddo, but its derivation and symbolic geography are debated. The historical Megiddo entry is a comparison, not proof that Revelation’s battle has a securely mapped location.

entries.title: Babylon falls: power, luxury & lament
entries.summary: A richly adorned woman called Babylon is shown in relation to the beast, and a great city’s fall draws grief from kings, merchants, and seafarers. Revelation exposes a world of seduction, exploitation, and violence against witnesses. Jeremiah’s earlier judgment on Babylon supplies language for a vision reaching beyond the ancient city alone.
entries.date: Vision sequence, not a dated schedule of future events
entries.note: Many historical readings associate this Babylon with Rome, drawing on the book’s imperial imagery. Other traditions extend or locate its fulfillment differently. No pin equates the visionary city with a single settled modern target.

echoes.label: Come out of her, My people
echoes.explanation: Jeremiah calls people out of historical Babylon. Revelation uses that language for its visionary city, keeping the question of allegiance in view.

entries.title: The marriage supper of the Lamb
entries.summary: After the lament over Babylon comes praise and an invitation to the marriage supper of the Lamb. Fine linen is explained as the righteous acts of the saints. An angel refuses John’s worship and directs him to God. The vision moves from the false city’s splendor toward a relationship of faithfulness and joy.
entries.date: Vision sequence, not a dated schedule of future events

entries.title: Faithful and True
entries.summary: Heaven opens, and a rider on a white horse is called Faithful and True, the Word of God, King of kings and Lord of lords. The sword comes from His mouth. This is Revelation’s vision of judgment and victory through the one the book has already shown as the slain Lamb, not an invitation for readers to wage private holy war.
entries.date: Vision sequence, not a dated schedule of future events

entries.title: A thousand years: read the vision carefully
entries.summary: Revelation describes Satan bound, a thousand-year reign, a release, and the final defeat of evil. The passage has produced major Christian disagreements over how its sequence relates to Christ’s return and the present age. The shared horizon is that evil does not reign forever and the witness of those who belong to Jesus is not forgotten.
entries.date: Vision sequence, not a dated schedule of future events
entries.note: Premillennial, amillennial, and postmillennial readings differ. This entry presents the chapter and names the disagreement; it does not assign the millennium a calendar start or declare one scheme proven.

entries.title: The books are opened
entries.summary: Before the great white throne, the dead stand and books are opened, including the book of life. Death and Hades themselves are thrown into the lake of fire. Daniel’s opened books return in a vision of final accountability. The story is moving toward a world where death is no longer at home.
entries.date: Vision sequence, not a dated schedule of future events

entries.title: Behold, I make all things new
entries.summary: A new heaven and a new earth appear, and the holy city comes down from God. The dwelling of God is with humanity; tears, death, mourning, crying, and pain pass away. The city has no temple because God and the Lamb are its temple, and the Lamb is its lamp. Scripture’s story of presence reaches a breathtaking homecoming.
entries.date: Vision sequence, not a dated schedule of future events

echoes.label: God’s dwelling with humanity
echoes.explanation: Compare the covenant dwelling in Ezekiel, Isaiah’s new creation, and the voice from Revelation’s throne. The Lamb—not a building—is the city’s temple and light.

entries.title: The tree of life, for the healing of nations
entries.summary: A river of the water of life flows from the throne of God and the Lamb. The tree of life bears fruit, and its leaves are for the healing of the nations. Genesis’s garden and Ezekiel’s river meet in a city without curse or night. The end does not forget the beginning: God’s servants see His face.
entries.date: Vision sequence, not a dated schedule of future events

echoes.label: The garden and the river return
echoes.explanation: Genesis gives a garden, river, and tree of life; Ezekiel gives healing water and fruitful trees. Revelation brings the river and tree into the city of God and the Lamb.

entries.title: The Spirit and the bride say, “Come.”
entries.summary: Jesus names Himself the Root and the Offspring of David, the bright morning star. The Spirit and the bride invite the thirsty to come and receive the water of life freely. The final response is not a solved timetable but a prayer: “Amen! Yes, come, Lord Jesus.” The book closes with His grace.
entries.date: Vision sequence, not a dated schedule of future events

entries.title: Mary · Jesus’ mother
entries.summary: Mary receives Gabriel’s announcement, sings of God’s mercy, and keeps the unfolding story in her heart. The Gospels place her at Cana and at the cross; Acts names her among those praying with the disciples. Her story reaches from the birth of Jesus into the waiting church.
entries.date: Birth often placed c. 6–4 BCE · exact chronology debated

entries.title: Joseph · Mary’s husband
entries.summary: Matthew portrays Joseph receiving Mary, naming Jesus, protecting the family, and responding to guidance in dreams. Luke names him in the family’s early journeys. He is distinct from the Joseph of Genesis and from Joseph of Arimathea; Matthew’s genealogy identifies him as Mary’s husband.
entries.date: Birth often placed c. 6–4 BCE · exact chronology debated

entries.title: Elizabeth
entries.summary: Elizabeth, wife of Zechariah and mother of John, receives a long-awaited child and welcomes Mary with blessing. Luke places her joy within the wider promise unfolding around Jesus. Her named relationship to Mary is kinship, not a precisely specified family tree.
entries.date: Birth often placed c. 6–4 BCE · exact chronology debated

entries.title: Zechariah · John’s father
entries.summary: A priest serving in the temple, Zechariah receives the announcement of John’s birth and responds with a question. His period of silence ends when he confirms the child’s name. His restored voice praises God’s redemption and names John’s work as preparing the Lord’s ways.
entries.date: Birth often placed c. 6–4 BCE · exact chronology debated

entries.title: Herod the Great
entries.summary: Matthew places the arrival of the magi and the threat against the child Jesus in the reign of Herod. The king’s fear of a rival contrasts with the visitors’ worship. This Herod is distinct from Herod Antipas, the later ruler connected with John the Baptist’s death and Jesus’ trial in Luke.
entries.date: Birth often placed c. 6–4 BCE · exact chronology debated

entries.title: Herod Antipas
entries.summary: The Herod associated with John’s imprisonment and death is the tetrarch Antipas, not the Herod of Matthew’s infancy story. Mark describes the banquet at which John is killed; Luke places Jesus before this ruler during the final proceedings in Jerusalem.
entries.date: Public ministry · commonly placed in the late 20s / early 30s CE

entries.title: Pontius Pilate
entries.summary: The Roman governor conducts proceedings against Jesus and authorizes His crucifixion. The Gospels describe questioning, political pressure, and a royal charge. Pilate’s official role belongs to the historical setting of Jesus’ death, distinct from the authority Jesus claims for His own kingdom.
entries.date: Passion and resurrection · commonly dated around 30 or 33 CE

entries.title: Simon Peter
entries.summary: Called from fishing into discipleship, Peter confesses Jesus as the Christ, misunderstands the way of the cross, denies Him, and receives a renewed commission. Acts follows his witness at Pentecost and his encounter with Cornelius. His courage and failure remain in the same story.
entries.date: Public ministry · commonly placed in the late 20s / early 30s CE

entries.title: Andrew
entries.summary: Andrew follows Jesus and brings his brother Simon to meet Him. John later shows him noticing the boy with loaves and fish and helping bring an approach from Greek visitors. His appearances often involve introducing someone else to Jesus.
entries.date: Public ministry · commonly placed in the late 20s / early 30s CE

entries.title: John · son of Zebedee
entries.summary: John is called with his brother James and appears with Peter and James at moments such as the transfiguration. Acts places Peter and John together in witness. Later traditions about the Fourth Gospel and Revelation should be distinguished from what these passages themselves name.
entries.date: Public ministry · commonly placed in the late 20s / early 30s CE

entries.title: James · son of Zebedee
entries.summary: James is called with John from their father’s boat and is present at the transfiguration. Acts reports his execution under Herod Agrippa. He is not the James associated with leadership in the Jerusalem council; recurring names need distinct identities.
entries.date: Public ministry · commonly placed in the late 20s / early 30s CE

entries.title: Thomas
entries.summary: John preserves Thomas’s readiness to accompany Jesus toward danger, his question about the way, and his difficulty believing the resurrection report. His encounter with the risen Jesus leads to the confession “My Lord and my God.” Doubt is part of his story, not its final definition.
entries.date: Public ministry · commonly placed in the late 20s / early 30s CE

entries.title: Mary Magdalene
entries.summary: Luke names Mary among women who supported Jesus’ ministry; the Gospels remember her at the crucifixion, burial, and resurrection discovery. John gives her the announcement “I have seen the Lord.” The texts do not identify her as the unnamed sinful woman of Luke 7.
entries.date: Public ministry · commonly placed in the late 20s / early 30s CE

entries.title: Paul · also called Saul
entries.summary: The persecutor who encounters Jesus becomes a witness among the nations. Acts narrates journeys, churches, disputes, imprisonment, and arrival in Rome; his letters speak into the lives of particular communities. Acts 13:9 says Saul was also called Paul, rather than describing a name change at his conversion.
entries.date: First-century settings · letters are grouped by theme, not asserted writing date

entries.title: Barnabas · son of encouragement
entries.summary: Barnabas shares resources, vouches for Saul, recognizes grace at Antioch, and travels in mission. Acts also records a sharp disagreement between him and Paul over John Mark. Encouragement and real disagreement both belong to the story of the early church.
entries.date: First-century settings · letters are grouped by theme, not asserted writing date

entries.title: James · a leader in Jerusalem
entries.summary: James speaks in the Jerusalem council after Peter, Barnabas, and Paul. Galatians identifies James the Lord’s brother among the leaders Paul met. He is distinguished here from James son of Zebedee, whose death is reported earlier in Acts.
entries.date: First-century settings · letters are grouped by theme, not asserted writing date

entries.title: Priscilla & Aquila
entries.summary: This couple works with Paul, travels, opens a household to a church, and helps Apollos understand the way of God more accurately. Their story shows teaching and hospitality woven into ordinary work. Paul calls them fellow workers in Christ Jesus.
entries.date: First-century settings · letters are grouped by theme, not asserted writing date

entries.title: Timothy
entries.summary: Acts introduces Timothy as a disciple with a Jewish believing mother and a Greek father. He joins Paul’s work; Paul speaks of him warmly in Philippians. Letters addressed to Timothy turn toward the care of teaching and communities, extending the story beyond travel into patient leadership.
entries.date: First-century settings · letters are grouped by theme, not asserted writing date

places.name: Ur
places.description: Traditionally identified with Tell el-Muqayyar in southern Mesopotamia; the location of Abraham’s Ur is debated.

places.name: Haran
places.description: The ancestral stop in northern Mesopotamia before Abram travels to Canaan.

places.name: Babylon
places.description: The Mesopotamian city associated with exile. Genesis’s Babel narrative is set in the land of Shinar; this pin is Babylon, not a located tower.

places.name: Nineveh
places.description: Assyrian city on the Tigris, opposite modern Mosul; central to Jonah and Nahum.

places.name: Mountains of Ararat
places.description: An approximate regional marker. Genesis 8:4 names the mountains of Ararat, not a confirmed landing site.

places.name: Mount Hermon
places.description: The mountain named in 1 Enoch 6 as the place of the Watchers’ oath.

places.name: Damascus
places.description: The Aramean capital; connected with Naaman, Hazael, and the northern kingdom.

places.name: Sidon
places.description: Phoenician coastal city. Jezebel is identified as the daughter of Ethbaal, king of the Sidonians.

places.name: Zarephath
places.description: Coastal town associated with the widow who shelters Elijah.

places.name: Mount Carmel
places.description: The Carmel ridge, setting of Elijah’s confrontation in 1 Kings 18; the exact spot is not established.

places.name: Jezreel
places.description: Royal city connected with Naboth’s vineyard, Ahab, Jezebel, and Jehu.

places.name: Megiddo
places.description: Strategic pass and city; Josiah meets Pharaoh Neco here in 2 Kings 23.

places.name: Samaria
places.description: Omri’s capital of the northern kingdom, identified with ancient Samaria at Sebastia.

places.name: Shechem
places.description: City between Ebal and Gerizim: Abraham’s altar, covenant renewal, and the kingdom’s division.

places.name: Bethel
places.description: Traditionally identified near Beitin; associated with Jacob’s dream and Jeroboam’s northern sanctuary.

places.name: Shiloh
places.description: Sanctuary associated with Hannah, Eli, Samuel, and the ark before its capture.

places.name: Jericho
places.description: The Jordan-valley city associated with Rahab and Joshua.

places.name: Jerusalem
places.description: David’s capital, Solomon’s temple, prophetic confrontation, and the Babylonian siege.

places.name: Bethlehem
places.description: Home associated with Ruth, Boaz, Jesse, and David.

places.name: Hebron
places.description: Abraham’s residence near Mamre and David’s first royal seat.

places.name: Beersheba
places.description: Southern ancestral center associated with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.

places.name: Valley of Elah
places.description: The valley associated with David’s encounter with Goliath; marker is regional.

places.name: Mount Gilboa
places.description: Mountain ridge where Saul and his sons fall in battle against the Philistines.

places.name: Gaza
places.description: Philistine city connected with Samson’s final imprisonment and death.

places.name: Ramoth-gilead
places.description: A contested Transjordanian city in the wars with Aram. This is an approximate regional marker, not a settled site identification.

places.name: Jabbok / Penuel region
places.description: The river region where Jacob wrestles before meeting Esau. Penuel’s exact identification is debated.

places.name: Jordan crossing region
places.description: Approximate river region opposite Jericho; not a reconstruction of a specific crossing route.

places.name: Moab
places.description: Regional marker east of the Dead Sea, associated with Ruth, Balaam, and Israel’s approach to the land.

places.name: Mount Nebo
places.description: Traditional identification of the mountain from which Moses views the land.

places.name: Nile Delta / Egypt
places.description: Regional marker for Israel’s Egyptian sojourn. No identification of the biblical Pharaoh is assumed.

places.name: Mount Sinai (traditional)
places.description: Jebel Musa is a traditional identification; the biblical mountain’s location is disputed. No Exodus route is asserted.

places.name: Kadesh-barnea (traditional)
places.description: Often identified in the Ain el-Qudeirat region. A regional guide to the wilderness stories, not a settled itinerary.

places.name: Lachish
places.description: Judahite city besieged by Sennacherib; a key setting in the Assyrian crisis.

places.name: Mizpah (traditional)
places.description: Often associated with Tell en-Nasbeh; connected with Samuel and Gedaliah. Identification is not certain.

places.name: Susa
places.description: Persian royal city associated with Esther and with Nehemiah’s service at court.

places.name: Nazareth
places.description: Galilean home of Jesus’ upbringing and setting of Luke’s synagogue scene.

places.name: Sea of Galilee
places.description: Regional lake marker for fishing, crossings, and Jesus’ Galilean ministry; not a precise location for every shoreline event.

places.name: Capernaum
places.description: Village on the northern shore of the lake, repeatedly associated with Jesus’ teaching and healing.

places.name: Cana (regional)
places.description: A regional Galilean marker. Several sites have been proposed for the Cana of John’s Gospel.

places.name: Nain (traditional)
places.description: Traditionally identified with Nein in lower Galilee; the setting of the widow’s son in Luke 7.

places.name: Sychar / Jacob’s well region
places.description: Regional guide near Shechem for John 4. Identification of Sychar and the precise relationship among sites is debated.

places.name: Caesarea Philippi
places.description: The northern district named in the accounts of Peter’s confession; distinct from the coastal Caesarea of Acts.

places.name: Bethany
places.description: Village east of Jerusalem associated with Martha, Mary, and Lazarus; distinct from the Bethany beyond the Jordan in John 1.

places.name: Mount of Olives
places.description: Ridge east of Jerusalem. Marker gives orientation, not a claim to locate every garden, teaching, or ascension scene precisely.

places.name: Tyre
places.description: Phoenician coastal city; the surrounding region appears in the encounter with the Syrophoenician woman.

places.name: Joppa
places.description: Coastal town where Acts places Peter’s stay with Simon the tanner and his vision.

places.name: Caesarea Maritima
places.description: Roman coastal city associated with Cornelius and Paul’s custody. Not Caesarea Philippi.

places.name: Antioch in Syria
places.description: The sending church of Acts 13; distinct from Pisidian Antioch.

places.name: Tarsus
places.description: Paul’s city of origin in Cilicia, identified in Acts 21:39 and 22:3.

places.name: Salamis, Cyprus
places.description: First Cypriot preaching stop named in Acts 13.

places.name: Paphos
places.description: Cypriot city associated with the encounter involving Sergius Paulus in Acts 13.

places.name: Pisidian Antioch
places.description: City of southern Asia Minor where Acts 13 records Paul’s synagogue address. Not Syrian Antioch.

places.name: Iconium
places.description: A city on the Acts 13–14 mission sequence, near modern Konya.

places.name: Lystra
places.description: Associated with the healing in Acts 14 and Timothy’s background in Acts 16; approximate ancient-site marker.

places.name: Derbe (approximate)
places.description: A southern Asia Minor stop named in Acts 14 and 16; marker reflects an approximate site identification.

places.name: Alexandria Troas
places.description: Aegean port associated with the Macedonian vision and later travel in Acts.

places.name: Philippi
places.description: Macedonian city associated with Lydia, the jailer, and the church addressed in Philippians.

places.name: Athens
places.description: Greek city where Acts 17 places Paul’s marketplace conversations and Areopagus address.

places.name: Corinth
places.description: Greek city associated with Paul, Priscilla and Aquila, and the Corinthian correspondence.

places.name: Ephesus
places.description: Roman Asian city prominent in Acts 19 and the first of Revelation’s seven messages.

places.name: Smyrna
places.description: Coastal city, now İzmir, addressed in Revelation 2:8–11.

places.name: Pergamum
places.description: City in western Asia Minor addressed in Revelation 2:12–17.

places.name: Thyatira
places.description: Lydia’s city of origin in Acts 16 and one of Revelation’s seven named cities.

places.name: Sardis
places.description: Ancient Lydian center addressed in Revelation 3:1–6.

places.name: Philadelphia in Asia
places.description: The ancient Asian city addressed in Revelation 3:7–13, not a modern American city.

places.name: Laodicea on the Lycus
places.description: City in the Lycus valley addressed in Revelation 3:14–22.

places.name: Patmos
places.description: Aegean island named by John as the setting of Revelation 1:9. Its visions are not geographic locations to plot.

places.name: Crete
places.description: Regional island marker for the voyage in Acts 27; not an asserted reconstruction of the ship’s track.

places.name: Malta
places.description: Island named in Acts 28 after the shipwreck. No specific landing cove is asserted here.

places.name: Rome
places.description: Imperial capital and the final setting of Acts. This geographical pin is not a claim that every use of “Babylon” means this location.

families.title: From Adam to Noah
families.description: The Sethite genealogy of Genesis 5. Enoch and Lamech here are distinct from their namesakes in Cain’s line. Only this selected line is shown.

families.title: Abraham’s household
families.description: A selected family tree: parent–child lines and named marriages. Other children and marriages are not exhaustively represented.

families.title: The children of Jacob
families.description: Children are grouped under their mothers; Jacob is father of each child shown. Dinah is included. Tribal allotment lists can count Joseph through Ephraim and Manasseh.

families.title: Ruth to the royal house
families.description: Selected generations in David’s family. The dashed line from Perez to Boaz skips generations explicitly listed in Ruth 4; it is not a direct parent–child claim.

families.title: Two houses entangled
families.description: Ahab’s northern dynasty meets Judah’s royal house through Athaliah. Her link to Ahab/Omri is deliberately not forced into a precise parent–child edge: Kings uses both kinship descriptions.

families.title: The promise leads to Jesus
families.description: A selected path through Matthew 1, not a complete genealogy. Long dashes omit generations. Mary is Jesus’ mother; Joseph’s distinct household/guardian line does not claim biological fatherhood. Luke 3 gives a different genealogy and is available for comparison.
